articles.title: Rains slow measles jab drive in Baguio; house-to-house campaign set
articles.summary: BAGUIO CITY — With measles vaccination coverage stuck at just 20 percent, the City Health Services Office (CHSO) is taking its campaign to the doorsteps of families as it races to immunize more…

blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY — With measles vaccination coverage stuck at just 20 percent, the City Health Services Office (CHSO) is taking its campaign to the doorsteps of families as it races to immunize more children amid weeks of heavy rains.

City health officials said additional workers from the Department of Health (DOH), CHSO and city health centers are being mobilized for house-to-house vaccinations across the city’s barangays, as the campaign remains far below its 95-percent target.
City Health Officer Dr. Celia Flor Brillantes attributed the low turnout to the prolonged rains, which have hampered vaccination activities.
“We will be saturating all our barangays through the help of our other health workers,” she said.

The DOH’s Measles-Rubella Supplemental Immunization Activity (MR-SIA) seeks to vaccinate at least 95 percent of children aged 6 months to below 5 years old, a coverage level considered crucial in limiting the spread of the highly contagious disease.

Brillantes appealed to parents and guardians who remain hesitant to have their children vaccinated, warning that failure to immunize them could leave them vulnerable to measles and its complications. She also warned that unvaccinated children could pose a risk to others, particularly those with weaker immune systems.
Health workers are expected to intensify the campaign in the coming week, with the CHSO hoping to substantially raise vaccination coverage through expanded outreach and house-to-house visits.
Meanwhile, records from the CHSO City Epidemiology and Surveillance Unit (CESU), under Medical Officer IV Donnabel Panes, showed that Baguio has recorded 22 measles cases, with no deaths reported.
Sixteen of the patients were male and six were female, with a median age of 1 year.—Maureen Matayew / Contributor /mr

articles.title: Puerto Galera residents warned of haze health hazards
articles.summary: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Residents and visitors of Puerto Galera have been advised to take health precautions as haze caused by smoke from Indonesian forest fires blankets the municipality,…

blocks.text: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Residents and visitors of Puerto Galera have been advised to take health precautions as haze caused by smoke from Indonesian forest fires blankets the municipality, the Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MDRRMO) warned on Friday, Sept. 4.
What may look like ordinary mist is actually a thick concentration of fine particles and pollutants that can cause a range of health problems, the MDRRMO said in an advisory.
Exposure to the haze may trigger eye irritation, coughing or sore throat, headaches, dizziness, difficulty breathing, asthma attacks, allergic reactions and fatigue, the office cautioned.
Children, older adults, pregnant women, individuals with allergies and outdoor workers are especially vulnerable and should take extra precautions.

“Minimizing exposure to polluted air is the best defense at this time,” the MDRRMO said, urging the public to stay indoors and keep doors and windows closed to prevent smoke from entering homes. Those who need to go outdoors should wear a properly fitting face mask to reduce the inhalation of airborne particles.

Motorists are also advised to keep vehicle windows closed and switch on the air-recirculation mode of their ventilation systems. Residents are likewise reminded to avoid smoking, burning garbage and other activities that add more smoke to the air.
Drinking plenty of water and refraining from strenuous outdoor physical activities are also recommended while haze conditions persist.

Residents are urged not to ignore serious symptoms. Anyone experiencing severe difficulty breathing, chest pain, prolonged coughing, severe headache or dizziness, confusion, or discoloration of the lips or face should immediately consult a doctor or proceed to the nearest health facility. INQ /mr

articles.title: Tate brothers charged with further trafficking and sex crimes in Romania
articles.summary: Andrew and Tristan Tate are currently in a Miami jail fighting extradition to the UK over separate charges and deny all the allegations.

blocks.text: The brothers - former kickboxers with dual US and British citizenship - have been under criminal investigation in Romania since December 2022.
They have been mainly based there since 2017, drawing a large social media audience - many of them young men - through misogynistic messages and images of a luxury lifestyle.
Many of the new charges centre on a vulnerable woman investigators allege was recruited by Tristan when she was 15.
She is alleged to have been sheltered in a building in Luton, Bedfordshire, for sexual exploitation by Andrew.
DIICOT investigators allege Andrew controlled her through surveillance and physical aggression and coerced her to perform sex acts on video chats for his financial gain.
He is also accused of moving her to Romania to carry on exploiting her in two of his homes.
Andrew is separately charged with having sex with a minor, who was 15, in Romania.
Prosecutors have also requested four of the brothers' luxury cars worth £710,000 are confiscated. They believe money was laundered through their purchase.
It is not yet clear if DIICOT will seek their extradition from the US, and the indictment has to be examined by a judge before any trial can open.
The Tates have denied all the allegations and say their online personas are not their real personalities.

Their lawyer Eugen Constantin Vidineac said: "Today's decision by DIICOT does not determine guilt and it should not be presented as though it does. It represents the prosecution's latest attempt to bring this case before a court following the failure of its previous indictment to proceed to trial.

"The history of these proceedings matters. The previous indictment was subjected to judicial scrutiny and the court identified significant irregularities which prevented the case from moving forward to trial.

"DIICOT has now chosen to file a new indictment. We will examine every aspect of it with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process.

"Our clients continue to reject the allegations against them. They have the right to the presumption of innocence, the right to properly examine the evidence relied upon against them and the right to mount an effective defence."

articles.summary:
A total fire ban is in place for greater Sydney with extreme fire danger exacerbated by hot and windy conditions

  • Get our
articles.byline: Australian Associated Press with Guardian staff

blocks.text: Summer heat is due to arrive early across much of eastern Australia with potentially record early September temperatures predicted for Brisbane and Sydney, while snow was expected in southern New South Wales.

Maximum temperatures in Sydney during the first days of September were on track to match the city’s midsummer average of 26.4C, warmer than any other start to spring since the city’s Observatory Hill station opened in 1858.
Suburbs across Sydney were expected to reach up to 33C on Saturday afternoon, smashing average September records by up to 13C.
The meteorologist Tom Saunders said a gusty north-westerly airstream blowing south from the northern interior would lift maximums this weekend by as much as 13C above the average.
The highest anomalies were set to affect the NSW coast.

“For Sydney, it’s likely to be the hottest day this early in spring on record and for the first five days of September we’re on track to average a top of 27 degrees that matches the midsummer average,” he told ABC News.
“Temperatures this spring will average as much as three degrees above the baseline from recent decades, potentially the hottest spring on record.”
The warm, dry and windy conditions would cause fire dangers to spike. A total fire ban was in place for the greater Sydney region, where extreme fire danger was forecast.

The dramatic – and potentially dangerous – start to Australia’s spring extended across much of the continent, with damaging winds that could bring down trees and roofs in South Australia, and minor to moderate flooding for parts of Victoria and Tasmania.
Meanwhile, in southern NSW, snow was on late Saturday morning falling in Thredbo in the Snowy Mountains.
The Bureau of Meteorology had forecast snowfall to hit Thredbo top station by 4pm on Saturday, with a daytime low temperature of -1C.
The new falls won’t do much to help the parlous cover remaining on Australia’s ski fields after a warm winter, however.

The Weatherzone journalist Anthony Sharwood on Friday wrote: “September snowfalls are meaningful when there’s a decent remnant snowpack from winter onto which the new snow can bond. But … the Australian snowpack is at a historic low for the first week of September, even at the highest elevations of the mountains.”
Across the border, southern Queensland would see temperatures peak in the mid-30s in another unseasonably warm start to September.
after newsletter promotion
In South Australia’s Mount Lofty and Flinders ranges, wind gusts of up to 110km/h were possible late Saturday into Sunday morning.
Heavy rains were forecast for north-east Victoria and northern Tasmania, with up to 60mm expected in some parts.
“The catchments in those areas are really wet,” the BoM meteorologist David Crock said on Friday. “They’ve seen multiple rounds of flood warnings this winter already.
“So we’ve got a flood watch current again for these catchments across northern Victoria … and across parts of northern Tasmania as well.”

The dramatic start to spring comes against the background of a “supersized” El Niño weather phenomenon to Australia’s east, one that is already breaking heat records, and could comfortably surpass previous events.

On Thursday, the UN’s weather agency said the event in the Pacific was continuing to strengthen and would probably persist until early 2027, warning it had the “potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world”.
El Niño events tend to mean hotter and drier conditions for Australia’s south and east in winter and spring, and can increase the risk of heatwaves, drought and bushfires.

Australia’s national council for fire and emergency services said fire authorities were predicting a heightened risk of fire across northern and south-eastern NSW, south-east Queensland, north-eastern Tasmania, parts of Western Australia, South Australia and Victoria, and large parts of the Northern Territory.

articles.title: Hospital bed shortage hits Oriental Mindoro
articles.summary: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — All public hospitals run by the provincial government are operating well beyond their authorized bed capacity due to various types of illnesses, resulting in a total…

blocks.text: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — All public hospitals run by the provincial government are operating well beyond their authorized bed capacity due to various types of illnesses, resulting in a total shortage of 187 beds as of Wednesday, Sept. 2, according to data from the Oriental Mindoro Provincial Health Office (PHO).
“All five hospitals are functioning beyond their limits, which stretches medical personnel, equipment, and space to the breaking point,” PHO head Dr. Cielo Ante told the Inquirer on Friday, Sept. 4.
Ante said the reasons for hospitalization include chronic diseases such as hypertension and diabetes, as well as respiratory infections, including cough and flu among children.

Combined, the five provincial health facilities have an authorized capacity of only 293 beds, but a total of 480 beds are currently occupied, translating to an overall occupancy rate of 163.8 percent.
The heaviest strain is seen at the Oriental Mindoro Southern District Hospital (OMSDH), which has just 46 authorized beds but is caring for 129 patients, resulting in a deficit of 83 beds.

The Oriental Mindoro Provincial Hospital (OMPH) in Calapan City, the province’s main referral hospital, is short of 51 beds, with 233 patients occupying space meant for 182. The Oriental Mindoro Central District Hospital (OMCDH) follows with a 43-bed shortage, serving 79 patients in a facility designed for 36.
Even smaller community hospitals are overwhelmed, with Naujan Community Hospital over capacity by nine beds and Bulalacao Community Hospital by one.

The bed shortage raises concerns over patient comfort, infection control, and the hospitals’ ability to accommodate new admissions, particularly amid ongoing health challenges and weather-related incidents across the province.
But Ante said the provincial government is currently constructing additional hospital wards and continuously hiring additional health workers.
“The PGOM also initiated efforts for the Mimaropa Regional Hospital in Brgy. Ilaya, which will give us an additional 300 to 500-bed capacity,” Ante said.
The hospitals also admitted suspected cases of leptospirosis following recent flooding in several areas of the province. INQ /mr

articles.title: What CHED’s student-athletes protection memo means after Ateneo tragedy
articles.summary: As varsity leagues nationwide seek to prevent another Ateneo tragedy, the Student-Athletes Protection Act aims to hold schools and sports associations more accountable

items: The tragic deaths of Ateneo basketball players Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili highlighted deficiencies in the university's athletic policies.

CHED's CMO No. 13 aims to regulate collegiate athletics and establish accountability among educational institutions, athletic associations, and stakeholders, emphasizing the protection and welfare of student-athletes.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
First of 2 parts

After a team-building activity in Dipaculao, Aurora, led to the deaths of Ateneo basketball players Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili on June 8, the tragedy exposed weaknesses in the university’s response, as well as gaps in its athletic policies and practices.

But just a week before the incident, the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) was set to operationalize Republic Act No. 10676, otherwise known as the Student-Athletes Protection Act, which was signed into law by former president Benigno Aquino III in 2015.
CHED’s Memorandum Order (CMO) No. 13, Series of 2026, signed on June 1, seeks to regulate collegiate athletic organizations.

“CMO 13 was not cited in the tragic Ateneo incident because it was not released prior to June 8, but it was already done by March,” said Dr. Lorenzo Lorenzo, the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) representative who helped draft the CMO.

“[Crafting the CMO] took us around six to eight months and was not only participated in by the NCAA and UAAP, but also almost all athletic associations in the country,” added Lorenzo, who’s also the vice president for administration of Emilio Aguinaldo College.
“We could say it was carefully studied, but it was quite unfortunate we were not able to use this measure during the incident.”
Section 9 of the decade-old law mandated CHED to operationalize it through a memorandum order, but it took the agency almost 11 years to release one.
“It is not a reaction to [the] Ateneo [tragedy]. Unfortunately, it was released late. Why? Of course, CHED had to go through many administrative procedures that’s quite complex,” Lorenzo said.

The CMO notes that one of its objectives is to “strengthen accountability among HEls [higher education institutions], Athletic Associations, Student-Athletes, other individuals or organizations, and all concerned stakeholders.”
Section 8 of the CMO also lists its scope, covering the student-athletes’ “activities, procedures, requirements, and processes,” whether “conducted on-campus or off-campus.”

The deaths of Baterbonia and Adili sparked public outrage and prompted probes, not just by the Ateneo de Manila University and the University Athletic Association of the Philippines (UAAP), but also by the National Bureau of Investigation, the Philippine National Police-Criminal Investigation and Detection Group, and the Senate.
Last August, the UAAP “perpetually banned” Ateneo men’s basketball coach Tab Baldwin and also indefinitely suspended team manager Epok Quimpo and several members of the coaching staff.
The Department of Labor and Employment, meanwhile, slapped Ateneo and Baldwin a P4.9-million administrative fine as the American-Kiwi coach lacked proper work permits.

“Very unfortunate, very tragic. We continue to mourn the loss of two lives. And it has derailed some of the best laid plans of mice and men, but nevertheless, we should not put the lives of Rene and Divine to waste,” said UAAP executive director Rebo Saguisag.
“We have to learn from it and we have to tighten our protocols, our rules, to ensure that it does not happen again. And I believe that’s one way of honoring the lives of Rene and Divine.”
NCAA basketball commissioner Rico Paolo Quicho said one of the salient points of CMO No. 13 is the “imposition of clear responsibilities” on schools, leagues, coaches, and administrators.
“[The CMO] establishes a comprehensive legal framework that places student-athletes — not competitions — at the center of collegiate sports governance,” said Quicho.

In sections 21 and 22, he noted, all public and private schools are “required to implement comprehensive student-athlete support systems,” including injury and death protocols, off-campus activity compliance, insurance coverage, and socio-emotional and mental health services.
The memorandum also states that incidents must be reported to their respective schools and the CHED within 48 hours, and investigations and appropriate penalties must be conducted within a week.
Findings must be submitted to the CHED within 15 days upon completion of the investigation.
“These practices should be, I believe, primarily under the purview of each of the member schools under the in loco parentis (in the place of a parent) rule,” said Saguisag.
“They’re the substitute parents while in their care. We, in the UAAP, are responsible during the games, and that is what we have been focusing on.”
Lorenzo said the NCAA, in compliance with the memorandum, has already set plans to teach sports officials and athletes basic safety protocols.

“What’s most important now is to ensure the safe competition environment. Right now, we’ve set a seminar on first aid; how to deliver first aid to players among referees and officials. So right then and there, they already know what to do,” he said.
Lorenzo recalled a 2024 incident in NCAA men’s basketball when Lyceum basketball star JM Bravo had a convulsion on court following an accidental head collision.

“If you remember, when he collapsed, nobody knew how to handle it right away,” Lorenzo said. “So now, we’ll have a seminar with the referees and the student-athletes. We’ll train them because the awareness and basic skills in first aid are important.”

“Aside from that, we’ll continue to strengthen our advocacy not just on-season, but also during preseason and postseason — that when they join competitions or leagues, they should ensure the safety standards and protocols of the players,” he added.

CHED said alongside the “protection and promotion of the rights and welfare” of student-athletes, the memorandum aims to address other issues in amateur leagues, including commercialization and exploitation.
“The memorandum reflects a significant policy shift by emphasizing institutional accountability,” Quicho said.

“Rather than placing the burden solely on student-athletes, it imposes affirmative duties on [higher educational institutions], athletic associations, coaches, administrators, and CHED itself to establish systems that promote academic success, physical and mental health, ethical sports governance, transparency, and effective grievance mechanisms,” he added.

Quicho said among the CMO’s “strongest innovation is its detailed regulation against commercialization,” as well as “unethical recruitment and poaching” and “retaliatory actions” by schools against transferring student-athletes.
CHED lists specific rules, mainly pointing out that “institutions bear primary responsibility for safeguarding student-athletes.” (To be concluded) – Rappler.com

articles.title: Judge refuses to block Pentagon from firing Stars and Stripes journalists
articles.summary:
Ruling allows defense department to proceed for now in exerting greater editorial control over military news outlet

A federal judge has declined to stop the Pentagon from firing journalists…

blocks.text: A federal judge has declined to stop the Pentagon from firing journalists who say they were illegally punished for speaking out about the need for the Stars and Stripes publication to maintain its editorial independence.
The ruling by US district judge Trevor McFadden allows the Pentagon to proceed for now in exerting greater editorial control over the historically independent military news outlet.

The journalists are unlikely to prove that the Pentagon violated their first amendment free speech rights, according to McFadden, a Donald Trump appointee. He said Stars and Stripes’ editorial independence “is not at stake here”.
“Plaintiffs argue that their termination will chill the protected expression of themselves and others at Stripes,” McFadden wrote. “Plaintiffs have failed to demonstrate a chill here.”

Stars and Stripes publisher Max Lederer, editor-in-chief Erik Slavin and Middle East reporter Lara Korte sued last Thursday in Washington DC, to challenge their firings by the Pentagon, which partially funds the news outlet.

The lawsuit says that Pentagon officials directed Lederer to fire Slavin and Korte after the publication of an 11 August article detailing deteriorating conditions and mental health crises aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln. Lederer declined to do so and later announced his retirement, saying the Pentagon had installed a new deputy publisher without his knowledge.
McFadden, however, concluded that Slavin and Korte were legally dismissed for giving interviews to CBS News as part of their official duties as public employees and not as private citizens.

“They are being fired for giving pre-approved interviews on their paper’s behalf in which they largely toed the company line,” the judge wrote. “Whatever else such a scheme may violate, it does not clearly offend the first amendment.”
The defense department and defense secretary Pete Hegseth are among the lawsuit’s named defendants.

McFadden’s ruling deals a blow to the journalists, whose lawsuit argues that they should be reinstated to their jobs. An attorney for the journalists called the ruling “disappointing”, according to CNN.
At least two other lawsuits accused the Pentagon of interfering with Stars and Stripes’s editorial integrity and independence.
Pulitzer-winning reporters Susan Dardarian and William Church, who serve as advisory board members to the publication, sued the Pentagon in June, accusing the military of illegal censorship.
The publication’s former ombudsman, Jacqueline Smith, sued the Pentagon the same month, saying she was fired in retaliation for an opinion column, in violation of her first amendment rights.

articles.title: Why are European countries moving their gold out of North America?
articles.summary: The Netherlands has relocated 86 tonnes of the shiny stuff - what's going on?

blocks.text: When the central bank of the Netherlands confirmed this week that it had moved tonnes of the country's gold out of North America, it said the relocation would make it "better prepared for severe crises".

Some 86 tonnes from the combined total of about 313 tonnes held in the US and Canada were relocated to London "in view of increasing geopolitical unrest", it said, so the shiny stuff could be "readily available for use in a crisis situation".
Questions were bound to follow. Why were the Dutch doing this? Were they anticipating some major economic shock on the horizon?

It seems not, but the move was clearly in response to the unstable and uncertain state the world finds itself in, with trade and military wars prompting countries to take precautions and hold their gold closer to home.

Earlier this year, France announced it had removed its gold reserves from the US to home shores. Meanwhile, Germany's Bundesbank transferred more than 216 tonnes of the metal from storage locations abroad - 111 tonnes from New York and 105 tonnes from Paris - over a few years ending in 2016., external

It is a strategy which has played out before in times of global instability. "Some European central banks moved part of their gold holdings to New York during the Cold War," said research analysts Lina Thomas and Daan Struyven of Goldman Sachs.

Joseph Cavatoni, senior market strategist at the World Gold Council, told the BBC while wars and trade tensions were "playing into some of these decisions", it didn't "top the list" of motivating factors.
Inflation, interest rates and just having gold in a place where it can be traded quickly also played a role.

"I don't get a sense that there's an impending doom," Cavatoni said, "but what I do think is people are being better educated around how to manage their reserve assets, growing their reserve assets, and actually thinking more effectively around how to make the most of those assets."
De Nederlandsche Bank said the gold removed from the US and Canada between March and August this year was now being held in the vaults of the Bank of England.
"We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness," said the governor of the Dutch central bank, Olaf Sleijpen.

London was seen as the best choice due its position in the world as a major trading centre. If you want to be able to buy or sell gold fast in a crisis, London is the place to be, which makes the Bank of England a popular storage spot.
The Bank is one of the largest custodians of gold in the world. Underneath the 300-year-old institution in central London sits about 400,000 bars worth more than £200bn.

According to industry surveys by the World Gold Council, the Bank of England remains the most popular vaulting location, but central banks are increasingly diversifying where they store the precious metal.
Where to store your country's gold is "increasingly top of mind for reserve managers", according to Thomas and Struyven of Goldman Sachs.

In the modern world, there are many ways to shift your treasure around. The Dutch sold about 59 tonnes in New York and then bought more stocks in London, meaning that amount didn't need to be hauled across the Atlantic.
But more than 27 tonnes were "physically transferred" from the US and Canada to the Dutch town of Zeist. A similar quantity was also sent from Zeist to London.

Companies that perform such services are tight-lipped on how operations are carried out, but it's fair to say the security measures and planning are extensive to avoid the risk of a real-life Italian Job.

Cavatoni, of the World Gold Council, said one standard approach to move gold stocks was to sell the commodity in one place and buy it in another. "Let's say I want my gold in New York and I have it in London. I could sell it in London, buy it in New York, same day, same time, effectively book transfer without actually having to put it on any other logistical change."

There are only a few select companies which handle gold shipments across borders, one of which is Brink's Global Services, who told the BBC it had seen "increased demand" from the likes of central banks in recent times.

"Heightened geopolitical and economic uncertainty, along with gold's growing role as a strategic reserve asset, appear to be contributing to this trend," said Nader Antar, Brink's executive vice president.

The reason gold storage is such a topic in the minds of central banks is because they have been increasingly buying the stuff. But storing it at home comes at a cost, said Thomas and Struyven of Goldman Sachs.
"Domestic storage requires investment in physical security, audit infrastructure, and insurance; costs that can be disproportionate for smaller central banks," they said.

Over the past four years, central banks have accumulated an annual average of 1,000 tonnes of gold, up significantly from the 500 tonnes average over the preceding decade, according to the World Gold Council.
The trend stretches back to the global financial crisis. And that is only expected to go up in the next year.
Gold has been having a moment in recent years. Its price has surged to hit a series of record highs, passing $5,000 an ounce in January.

There are several reasons behind its value jumping, but a major factor has been the precious metal's position in the human psyche as a so-called safe haven asset, to invest during periods of financial and geopolitical turmoil caused through trade and military wars.

Inflation and interest rates also influence gold's popularity. Due to the commodity's scarcity and the value placed on it across thousands of years, it is somewhat resistant against rising prices, and so is seen as a good investment.
"Over the past half-century, gold prices have risen much faster than the Consumer Price Index (CPI) - the most closely watched measure of inflation," according to investment bank Charles Schwab.
While the price of gold has fallen from the record high seen early this year, it still remains at a high level historically.
According to researchers at Goldman, the price is forecast to rise to $4,900 (£3,624) per troy ounce by the end of 2026, $300 more than it was in August.
The demand for gold from central banks is one key reason why prices are surging, according to Thomas and Struyven.

articles.title: Habagat rains to persist over Luzon, Visayas on Saturday
articles.summary: The southwest monsoon or habagat will continue to bring rains over parts of Luzon and Visayas on Saturday, September 5, with some areas expected to experience heavy downpours, state weather bureau…

blocks.text: September 5, 2026 | 9:36am

MANILA, Philippines — The southwest monsoon or habagat will continue to bring rains over parts of Luzon and Visayas on Saturday, September 5, with some areas expected to experience heavy downpours, PAGASA said.

The state weather bureau said that monsoon rains will prevail over Occidental Mindoro, while occasional rains are expected in Metro Manila, Zambales, Bataan, Tarlac, Pampanga, Bulacan, Rizal, Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Oriental Mindoro and Antique.

The Ilocos Region, Bicol Region, Western Visayas, the rest of Central Luzon, CALABARZON and MIMAROPA, as well as Abra, Benguet and Northern Samar, will have cloudy skies with scattered rain showers and thunderstorms.
The rest of Luzon will generally have partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms.
In Visayas, occasional rains are expected over Antique, while Western Visayas and Northern Samar may experience cloudy skies with scattered rain showers and thunderstorms.
The rest of the Visayas and the entire Mindanao will have generally fair weather, although hot and humid conditions are expected. Localized thunderstorms may still develop over Mindanao.
The weather in the rest of Luzon is expected to improve, although partly cloudy to cloudy skies may persist.
Heavy rainfall outlook
Occidental Mindoro may receive 100 to 200 millimeters of rain on Saturday due to the habagat.

PAGASA warned that flooding is likely, particularly in urbanized, low-lying areas and communities near rivers. Landslides are also possible in areas that are moderately to highly susceptible to the hazard.
Meanwhile, 50 to 100 mm of rain may fall over Zambales, Tarlac, Pampanga, Bulacan, Rizal, Metro Manila, Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Oriental Mindoro and Antique.
Localized flooding is possible in urbanized and low-lying areas and those near rivers, while landslides may occur in highly susceptible areas.
On Sunday, 50 to 100 mm of rain is expected over Zambales, Bataan, Tarlac, Pampanga, Cavite, Batangas and Occidental Mindoro.
For Monday, September 7, PAGASA expects the same rainfall range over La Union, Pangasinan, Benguet, Zambales, Bataan, Tarlac, Pampanga, Cavite, Batangas and Occidental Mindoro.
Tropical depression outside PAR
Meanwhile, PAGASA is monitoring a tropical depression located 1,685 kilometers east-northeast of Extreme Northern Luzon, outside the Philippine area of responsibility.
The tropical depression has maximum sustained winds of 55 kilometers per hour and gustiness of up to 70 kph.
It is moving northward at 35 kph, with its chances of entering PAR becoming increasingly low, according to PAGASA.

articles.title: US envoys to visit Russia, Ukraine with plan 'to end war'
articles.summary: Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are set to travel to Russia and Ukraine to revive peace talks. The trip would be the pair's first visit to Kyiv since Trump's reelection.

image.caption: In addition to peace efforts in the Middle East, Kushner and Witkoff (from left) are also working to end the war in Ukraine [File: April 2026]Image: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump said he was sending his son-in-law Jared Kushner and businessman Steve Witkoff to Moscow and Kyiv with a proposal to end the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"They're bringing with them a proposal to end the war," Trump told reporters Friday when asked about the pair's trip. Kushner and Witkoff have served as Trump's envoys to lead peace efforts in the Middle East as well as Ukraine.

The US president did not provide any details on the potential plan, including whether it involved Ukraine giving territory to Russia as he has previously suggested, instead, he said, "We have an idea for peace."
Kushner and Witkoff's first trip to Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that Kushner and Witkoff would travel to Ukraine on Sunday following talks in Moscow.

Recent media reports have questioned whether the pair would indeed travel to Ukraine. Despite trips to Moscow to meet with Russian officials, the US envoys have not visited Kyiv since Trump's reelection last year.

Trump had promised to end the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, on his first day back in office, but has more recently commented that bringing an end to the war was more complicated than he expected. In the past, he has blamed Ukraine for the Russian invasion and a "personality problem" between the countries' leaders for the continued fighting.

blocks.caption: Kushner and Witkoff met with Russia's Putin (left) in January; they have not been to KyivImage: Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool Photo via AP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Zelenskyy vows to pause air attacks during talks
Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram that Ukraine would halt airstrikes during the negotiations and called on Moscow to do the same so talks could proceed safely.

"As with previous diplomatic visits by the American side, we will ensure the normal functioning of Russian airspace so that the negotiators can arrive safely. We are concerned about their safety, not about Russia," Zelenskyy said.

Russian presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov did not confirm reports that US officials would visit Moscow, saying only that the media would be informed if such a meeting took place. Kushner and Witkoff were last in Moscow in January for a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
On Wednesday, Putin described negotiations as "frozen."
Drone strikes continue
Meanwhile, a Russian drone hit the headquarters of Ukraine's domestic security service (SBU) in Kyiv on Friday.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the strike "a major escalation" of the war.
"Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace — laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy," he wrote on X.
Zelenskyy said he ordered "an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike."
Ukraine has also launched repeated drone strikes on Russian oil infrastructure and the retail giant Wildberries.

articles.title: Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?
articles.summary: The AI-powered cameras have been vandalised across the US, as citizens object to the growing surveillance network.

blocks.text: Houston's historic Old Braeswood neighbourhood is affluent and tree-lined.
These are not the kind of streets where you would expect to see coordinated vandalism. Yet here four surveillance cameras were attacked and cut down in the middle of the night.

The metal poles were severed, leaving the distinctive black oval cameras and accompanying solar panels lying on the ground. On some of the cameras was a red sign reading: "Notice. 24/7 video recording".

These cameras are run by a company called Flock Safety and this sabotage, which happened in late July, is a signal of growing concern over the nationwide spread of sophisticated AI-powered surveillance systems. Similar vandalism incidents have occurred in Minnesota, California, and Georgia.

Proponents say they have made communities safer, and helped dramatically increase the rate at which crimes are solved. But recent examples of misuse have led some to worry. Critics say the cameras, which take pictures of the rear of every car that drives past, are overly broad investigative tools that treat civilians like suspects.

They see the little black poles popping up in their neighbourhoods as visible reminders of state power, at a time when public confidence in institutions is historically low and many are concerned about the accelerating pace of technological change and the influence of AI on people's lives.

items: Listen: ‘Big Surveillance’, Flock and ICE

blocks.text: Founded in 2017, Flock Safety has become one of the country's biggest makers of Automatic Licence Plate Readers (ALPRs). These AI-powered cameras take a picture of the rear of every car that drives past. Footage is retained for a specified amount of time.

But little is known about the extent that Flock is being used - the company does not publish exact data, but says it works with more than 7,000 communities nationwide, and estimates there are approximately 100,000 cameras deployed.

Records obtained by the BBC provide a rare glimpse into the extensive network of cameras and surveillance tech being used in America's fourth largest city, Houston, including the use of controversial facial recognition software powered by artificial intelligence.

Flock is not just selling cameras - it is selling access to a database that can include thousands of cameras from around the country. Older ALPRs did not have this vast network, which is a major selling point for law enforcement.
For example, Houston's METRO Transit Authority owns 35 cameras. But documents show METRO has access to around 20,000 devices in the Flock network - including some as far as Albany County, New York.

And as Flock expands, so too can the scope of investigations. Documents released to the BBC show how the network has grown year on year. In the Cypress-Fairbanks independent school district, a typical licence plate lookup in April 2024 searched around 270 networks of cameras.
By April 2025, the typical search scope had almost doubled to around 500 networks. In April 2026, 20% of searches were conducted across more than 6,000 networks.

Critics in Houston say this national network concerns them more than individual cameras. Christopher Rivera, from the Texas Civil Rights Project, worries that authorities could use "these databases to search our everyday routines, which ultimately scrapes out our routes to work, where our children go to school, and where we worship. And that's very problematic".

There have been recent incidents of privacy breaches that have caught national attention. Last week, a police officer in Kentucky was charged after using the Flock system to track his ex-girlfriend - who filed a protection order - over 2,000 times.
He was caught using Flock's newly mandatory, AI-powered audit tool that flags suspicious use.

Others are concerned about Flock being a way for police to avoid warrants, which are usually required to search a person's property or tap their phone. In 2025, a detective in Johnson County, Texas, searched over 80,000 images to locate a woman suspected of having an abortion. He did not have a warrant.

CCTV cameras, licence plate readers, and surveillance are not new. But the scale of Flock's network and the integration of AI in modern surveillance tech is a recent development and it's turned Flock into a household name. Americans who otherwise ignored the cameras in their cities have started to notice, and tune in to the capabilities of the technology around them.
With AI, unlike older licence-plate readers, law enforcement can search surveillance footage with a string of words like "Caucasian man, blue shirt" - not just a licence-plate image.

One thing Flock does not use is facial recognition. But that doesn't mean police departments are avoiding that tech. Critics say it violates human rights, is susceptible to misidentifying innocent people, and can be biased against minorities.

The BBC has received documents revealing that Harris County Sheriff's Office, which covers Houston, uses other facial recognition technology, Clearview AI. The tool includes a database of over 70 billion images, many of which were scraped from public internet sources including social media. The documents, including purchase orders and a License Agreement, show that the county's Clearview AI contract currently runs through to March 2027.
Several European countries have issued the company with data protection fines, including a £7.5m penalty from the UK's Information Commissioner.
Harris County Sheriff's Office use of this facial recognition technology has not been reported before. The office did not respond to requests for comment.
Police say surveillance technology like this, including Flock cameras, is important for fighting crime.

"It's a very good tool," says Chief Ray Schultz of the Memorial Villages Police Department - a small jurisdiction within Houston. "It makes the community safer." Before purchasing a Flock ALPR, his department would recover an average of three stolen cars a year. Now, this figure is 45, Schultz says.

Some crimes solved in recent years would have been "impossible" without Flock, he adds. Last month, Schultz used the tool to find an elderly woman with dementia who had driven 60 miles from Galveston to Houston and had got lost. "We were able to find her and reunite her with her family."
Schultz says that it is important for agencies to have strong policies governing ALPR use and officers that misuse the system should be held accountable.
"But don't throw out a tool that is valuable, that can help recover a missing child."
Jasmine Khadem Gonzalez, an immigrant rights organiser, is worried that law enforcement might "use [the Flock] database to tell ICE where somebody is".

The federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency does not have a contract with Flock directly. However, there have been reports of police officers citing "immigration" or "ice" as a reason for searching a licence plate.

Jessie, an immigrant from Central America, noticed a Flock camera outside her house last month. She asked the BBC to not use her real name out of fear it could impact a pending case to extend her green card.
"It makes me feel as if I'm being stalked," she says.
In response, she's changed her commute to work: "I try to take different routes every day so there's not a pattern."

But whether individual law enforcement agencies share info with the federal government is unclear. Federal immigration enforcement cannot access Flock data directly, Flock's CEO says. But some police departments have standing agreements with federal immigration enforcement to work together.

In Harris County, a proposed Flock contract amendment initially included the explicit authorisation to share camera data with federal law enforcement, but this provision was later removed after push-back from campaigners.
Some jurisdictions have opted not to renew contracts with Flock as a result of these concerns, including large metropolitan areas like Los Angeles, Seattle, and Austin, Texas.

In total, over 200 communities have cancelled or not renewed their contracts since 2021 - including 90 in the month of August alone - according to advocacy group Secure Justice, external. Their reasons for cancelling may include cost and concerns about data privacy.

Nationally, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have suggested there ought to be guardrails and several candidates have made it a campaign issue for the upcoming midterms. Republican Congressman Keith Self has proposed legislation that would require federal agencies to get warrants before accessing Flock data.

The company itself has also amended some of its policies, such as requiring mandatory audits, and reducing the default period that data stays on a server from 30 days to 7 days, unless flagged as part of an investigation. But individual agencies can choose to retain data for much longer.
Flock Safety's CEO and founder, Garrett Langley, told the BBC it's up to individual cities to decide how long to store data, and what information to share with whom.
"I don't think a technology company should be making decisions like that," he says.
"As long as it's a lawful investigation, we are not going to tell cities what laws they should or should not enforce."
Flock is a safety, not surveillance, company, Langley says. Yet three patents filed between 2020 and 2025 have the word "surveillance" in the title.
He boasts that the tech helped solve "about a million crimes" and helped find over 10,000 missing people.
"The debate of how we build a society where safety and privacy coexist" is worth having, he says, but the ongoing vandalism is "disappointing".
But there is nothing Flock or law enforcement could say to make Jessie feel at ease with this technology, she says. "I just don't trust that they're doing it to keep us safe."

articles.title: Trump order directs officials to consider stripping protections for gray wolves
articles.summary:
Interior department given three months to decide whether wolves can be removed from endangered species list

Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday directing the interior department…

blocks.text: Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday directing the interior department to consider de-listing gray wolves from the Endangered Species Act and to contemplate whether the agency could make it easier to authorize killing them.
The order gives interior secretary Doug Burgum three months to determine whether gray wolves and Mexican gray wolves have recovered enough for the federal government to de-list them.

But the US Fish and Wildlife Service, a division of the interior department, has already attempted to de-list the gray wolf – a decision that is currently tied up in litigation. A 2022 federal court order has left wolves protected by the ESA across most of their range in the lower 48 states.
The major exception is in the northern Rocky Mountain states of Montana, Idaho and Wyoming, where states manage wolves. In Minnesota, wolves are classified as “threatened” rather than “endangered”.
The USFWS has not attempted to de-list the Mexican gray wolf, a rare sub-species that was reintroduced to New Mexico and Arizona in 1998.

The current recovery plan for Mexican gray wolves requires a population average of more than 320 animals for four years in a row before federal authorities consider de-listing. Arizona and New Mexico counted a total of 319 animals at the end of 2025, triggering the first year in which officials can start counting to make the case for de-listing.

But Mexican gray wolves also face dire threats from lack of genetic diversity, according to Michael Robinson, an advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. Premature de-listing, he said, would likely invite challenge from environmental groups.
“We’re going to be fighting every step of the way, with information, with science,” Robinson said. “That should be the core of the decision-making process.”
Trump’s order also directs federal authorities to urge states to remove protections for gray wolves and loosen local restrictions on wolf killing.
The order drew sharp criticism from environmental groups.

“Once again, we see this administration attempting to override the checks and balances provided by bedrock environmental laws like the Endangered Species Act in order to create industry carveouts and distract from other bad policies that are proving unpopular,” said Leia Barnett, New Mexico conservation lead for WildEarth Guardians.

“Directing federal agencies to pressure states into rolling back their own wildlife protections isn’t just bad policy, it’s an attempt to bypass the very framework Congress built to keep species recovery decisions insulated from political whims.”

The federal government systematically trapped and killed wolves in the US through the late 19th and early 20th centuries, pushing them to the brink of extirpation from the contiguous states, largely to protect livestock from predation.

Ranchers still largely view the animals as a nuisance that threatens their already slim profit margins. Trump’s order was part of a broader series of measure aimed at protecting ranchers and American beef production.
Trump appeared to suggest his order would make it easier to shoot wolves, despite the fact that most of them remain protected.
“You can shoot them as of today?” Trump asked at the signing ceremony, referring to Mexican gray wolves while talking with an Arizona rancher.
The comment drew laughter. US agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins interjected to say that interior secretary Burgum “has to do a little magic, but yes”.
Gray wolves are protected under the Endangered Species Act across most of their range in the lower 48, making it a federal crime to kill one in most cases, regardless of Trump’s order.

But Trump raised the issue again at the signing ceremony. A rancher told the president that people in his home state of Washington struggle with wolves, noting that in one case a pack of wolves caused a young girl to climb a tree to safety.
“You’re allowed to go and take care of it,” Trump told the rancher.
“If you say so, sir,” he replied.
“We have no choice,” Trump said. “I’ve been hearing about it for a long time.”

articles.title: After 12 years of fried chicken and flirting, hit YouTube series Chicken Shop Date to end
articles.summary: After more than a decade of interviewing and flirting with movie stars, musicians and athletes while sharing some fried chicken, Amelia Dimoldenberg, the host of the popular YouTube talk show Chicken…

image.caption: Amelia Dimoldenberg announced this week her popular YouTube Series Chicken Shop Date is coming to an end after 12 years and dozens of celebrity interviews. (Rebecca Cabage/Invision/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

After more than a decade of interviewing and flirting with movie stars, musicians and athletes while sharing some fried chicken, Amelia Dimoldenberg, the host of the popular YouTube talk show Chicken Shop Date, announced this week she's closing up shop.
Creator Amelia Dimoldenberg interviewed dozens of celebrities, including some Canadians

"To me the show is my very own romcom and I have loved creating so many stories for you to watch. I am so grateful to everyone who has followed me on this journey and found some joy in these episodes," Dimoldenberg wrote in an Instagram post on Thursday.

"I never thought I'd stop Chicken Shop Date, I thought maybe it would be a part of me forever, and in some way it always will, but I feel like it's now time to move on from this adventure and onto a new one."

Dimoldenberg started the show 12 years ago, interviewing musicians in Britain's underground rap scene. Since then, she's gone on to chat with celebs, including Keke Palmer, Conan O'Brien, Paul McCartney and Jack Harlow and garnered close to 3.5 million subscribers to her YouTube channel.

Chicken Shop Date follows a simple format: Dimoldenberg goes on a date of sorts with a celebrity at a fried chicken shop in London and asks them a blend of questions that are flirty, funny and sometimes awkward.

It produces the type of banter you'd more likely expect on a first date than a typical sit-down, talk show style interview. In some cases, like her 2024 sit-down with Andrew Garfield, it's led to what seemed to be some actual flirting.
"This is called flirting, Amelia, this is called flirting," Garfield says at one point.

Dimoldenberg also has some Canadians among her dozens of interviews. That includes Ryan Reynolds, whom Dimoldenberg corrects when he gives the wrong name for the character his wife Blake Lively played on Gossip Girl.
"That is right, Brooke from Gossip Girl loves you," Reynolds tells Dimoldberg, hinting at Lively's fandom of her show. At that point, Dimoldenberg points out Lively's character was named Serena.
"I don't think there is a Brooke," Dimoldenberg says.
Shania Twain also sat down for a date with Dimoldenberg in 2023, where Twain revealed that she'd never actually met Brad Pitt (despite mentioning him in her hit song That Don't Impress Me Much).

The massive success of her YouTube channel has led to opportunities for Dimoldenberg outside the chicken shop, including working the red carpet at the Oscars this year, where she interviewed another Canadian, Hudson Williams.

It's unclear what Dimoldenberg's next move is after Chicken Shop Date, but it appears she has some irons in the fire. She's currently signed on to develop a young adult drama series for the BBC, according to Deadline.
But in her goodbye post on Instagram, Dimoldenberg also promised "a few final dates" before ending the show for good.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sarah Petz is a Toronto-based senior writer with the CBC News live pages team. Born and raised in Manitoba, her career has taken her across three provinces, multiple cities and to northern Uganda.

articles.title: [Vantage Point] Why gov’t should slow down on the BI-Securiport P192-billion revenue deal
articles.summary: There's something fundamentally odd about the government’s plan to charge international travelers another US$4 every time they enter or leave the Philippines

items: The Bureau of Immigration plans to implement a 20-year border-security deal funded by a $4 fee on international travelers, projected to generate P192 billion, despite existing investments in biometric technology.

Concerns have been raised about the transparency of the project, including the financial model, cost adjustments, and potential duplication of existing systems already funded by the government and private entities.

Congress is investigating the implications of the fee, questioning the separation of aviation security costs from broader national security functions, and emphasizing the need for clarity on what travelers are actually paying for.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

The Bureau of Immigration (BI) wants travelers to finance a 20-year border-security deal projected to generate P192 billion, even as the government and the New NAIA Infra Corp. (NNIC) are already spending billions on biometric and immigration technology. Before signing with Securiport, government should show passengers exactly what they are paying for—and why.
I find something fundamentally odd about the government’s plan to charge international travelers another $4 every time they enter or leave the Philippines.

Four dollars may look harmless. But an ordinary round trip means $8, or roughly P500. Multiply that by millions of passenger movements and this becomes a multibillion-peso revenue stream financed by travelers.
And the deeper I looked into the proposed Civil Aviation and Immigration Security Services project, or CAISS, the more red flags I found.

blocks.caption: Screenshot from List of PPP projects in the pipeline as of June 3, 2024, ppp.gov.ph

blocks.text: Appearing before the House on August 24 (watch video below), Immigration Commissioner Joel Anthony Viado (starts from around 1:04:36) defended the project. He said US-based Securiport LLC would finance the P10.744-billion project, upgrade the technology every four years and train Immigration personnel.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] Why gov’t should slow down on the BI-Securiport P192-billion revenue deal

blocks.text: Government, in other words, would not initially write the check.

Viado said CAISS could generate P192 billion over its 20-year life. Under the basic $4 user fee, Securiport gets $3.80, or 95%, while BI gets $0.20, or 5%, plus an additional premium once annual passenger volume exceeds 50 million.

But even $4 is not necessarily the ceiling. BI’s tender documents obtained by Vantage Point call it a reference user fee that may be adjusted for inflation, material foreign-exchange movements or expansion of project scope. The adjustment mechanics are contained in the still-undisclosed Public-Private Partnership (PPP) agreement.
So does P192 billion already include those escalators? What passenger growth does it assume? How much will Securiport invest as equity and how much might it borrow?
The answers should exist.

BI’s tender requires financial projections through 2046 covering revenues, operating expenses, borrowings, debt repayments, equity contributions, payments to shareholders, project IRR, equity IRR and weighted average cost of capital.
There is a financial model behind this deal. Passengers simply have not seen it.

Even the project cost has moved dramatically. PPP Center records carried CAISS at P16.89 billion in March 2025. It then fell to P12.86 billion and eventually to the P10.744 billion approved by the Department of Justice in December—a reduction of P6.15 billion, or 36%.
Lower cost may reflect successful negotiation. But what changed? Scope? Equipment? Prices? Financing assumptions? And if project cost fell that much, how was the $4 fee recalibrated?
Then there is what government already has.

Since September 2024, New NAIA Infra Corp., the San Miguel-led consortium, has operated and modernized NAIA. As of August 15, NNIC had already remitted P78 billion to government while spending another P6.8 billion on rehabilitation and modernization.
NNIC funded 78 biometric Immigration e-gates at NAIA and deployed 517 other biometric-enabled passenger-processing units, although these are not all immigration systems.

BI itself already operates the UN-supported goTravel Advance Passenger Information System, which screens travelers against international watchlists before arrival. In July, that system detected an INTERPOL-listed passenger more than nine hours before his flight reached NAIA.

BI is also implementing a government-funded biometric modernization program incorporating an Automated Biometric Identification System and border-data exchange platform. In August, Viado separately awarded another P219-million government-funded project for advanced facial recognition and monitoring.

Does this sound duplication to you? Indeed, CAISS is considerably more ambitious, encompassing API/PNR (Advance Passenger Information/Passenger Name Record) processing, risk targeting, international databases, and advanced facial searches.
But that makes disclosure more important.
What stays? What gets integrated? What gets migrated or replaced? And what exactly does Securiport provide that government and NNIC have not already paid for?

BI’s own Strategy 2026–2040 raises another question. It identifies continuing border-modernization requirements and says the Immigration Trust Fund can finance licenses, hardware refreshes, biometric and risk-model updates, cybersecurity, and even AI-assisted risk analytics.
Why commit travelers to a private fee for 20 years before explaining why BI’s own modernization and funding mechanisms cannot provide some of the same capabilities?
International experience gives me another reason for caution.
In July, Sierra Leone suspended the $25 passenger security fee attached to its Securiport arrangement while government reviews the contract and an independent special audit proceeds.
The Gambia’s National Audit Office also scrutinized its Securiport arrangement and warned about termination costs associated with its long concession.
This demonstrates why scrutiny must happen before, not after, a long-term passenger-funded agreement is signed.

There is also a matter of principle. The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) allows legitimate aviation-security costs to be recovered from users under appropriate conditions. But its charging policies distinguish those costs from broader state functions such as intelligence gathering and national security, which civil aviation should not be made to finance.
CAISS expressly includes passenger intelligence, watchlist screening, and risk targeting.
So which part of the $4 pays for chargeable aviation services and which finances sovereign national-security functions?

Congress is asking similar questions. House Resolution 1064 seeks an investigation into the passenger fee, the “privatization of border security functions” and potential data-privacy and national-security risks.
Viado says no formal PPP contract has been signed. As of September 2, the PPP Center still lists CAISS as under comparative challenge, and BI has posted no Notice of Award.
Good. There is still time.

Publish the financial model and show us the passenger assumptions, debt, equity, operating costs, shareholder returns and escalation formula. Reconcile the P16.89-billion, P12.86-billion and P10.744-billion project costs, and map CAISS against the border systems government and NNIC are already funding.
Only then can government convincingly explain why passengers should finance the difference for the next 20 years.
Government may call CAISS a no-cost project because private capital supplies the money upfront, but as Milton Friedman famously put it, “There’s no such thing as a free lunch.”

Someone always pays. At NAIA, government already has a private concessionaire investing billions in modernization while remitting P78 billion to the state. Before it reaches for another P500 from every international round-trip traveler—and potentially more as the reference fee escalates—it owes passengers a simple answer: What exactly are we buying that we have not already paid for?
Privatization was supposed to take the burden off government. It was never supposed to keep putting that burden back on the passenger. – Rappler.com
