articles.title: Trump’s ‘retribution’ could now include Falklands as favor to Milei – and revenge on the UK
articles.summary:
US president suggests he might support his Argentinian acolyte’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islands

Donald Trump…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has long embraced vengeance. “I am your retribution,” he declared to an admiring audience at the 2023 Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) as he commenced his march back to the White House.
It is unlikely Argentina, and far-flung holdovers of the former British empire, were on the US president’s mind at the time.
But the tide of international events in the past three and a half years have turned Trump’s vindictive mindset to the advantage of Javier Milei, the boisterous rightwing Argentinian president.

Trump’s notorious fixation with payback was almost entirely the trigger for Milei’s televised address to his fellow Argentinians on Thursday, as he stated his intention to reopen his country’s claim to a set of windswept islands in the south Atlantic – known to Britain as the Falklands, and to Argentina as the Malvinas.

The centuries-old dispute over the islands’ sovereignty has lain dormant since 1982, when the two countries fought a brief, but bloody, conflict that began after Argentina’s ruling military dictatorship invaded the territory.

Britain reclaimed them after troops in a naval taskforce dispatched by the then prime minister, Margaret Thatcher – ironically lionized by Milei as a political exemplar and inspiration – stormed the territory and eventually forced Argentina’s surrender.

An uneasy peace has reined in the generation since, although Argentina, which returned to democracy the year after the conflict, has never renounced its claim to the isles – despite the adamant insistence of their less than 2,000 inhabitants that they remain British.

This week, however, Trump suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falkland Islands. Why would the president go out on a limb to threaten this fragile peace? And why now?
Milei jumped on Trump’s comment that he was “reviewing” the US’s longstanding neutral stance on the territory’s sovereignty, which amounts to a de facto recognition of Britain’s control.

Fueling Trump’s animus is grievance that Britain, under former prime minister Keir Starmer, declined to support the US president’s decision to go to war on Iran, another irony given that country’s deep-rooted suspicions of Britain and its imperial past.

The president’s obsession that allies declined to help him in a war he never consulted them on runs deep and wide – from Westminster to Seoul – and has the potential to upend US relationships around the globe, if unchecked.
And Milei’s attempt to capitalize on Trump’s vengeance underlines the potential for ripple effects of this war to reach waters far beyond the Gulf.
In what has become a repetitive refrain, Trump laid bare his sense of wounded affront in an interview with a rightwing British cable channel on Thursday.

“Your country was not there to help me,” he told GB News. “We didn’t need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, ‘Why don’t you send a couple of ships?’ He said, ‘We don’t have any.’ It was pretty sad, the whole thing.”

Milei’s opportunism could also be used by Trump as a bargaining chip – to lever more money from the cash-strapped UK treasury for defense spending and Nato contributions, after the new British chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, recently suggested that it might not reach increased spending targets.

It is a sorry pass for the “special relationship”, fostered through alliances in two worlds wars and deepened during the cold war and subsequent conflicts. Yet Britain is hardly alone in feeling the heat of a wrathful Trump.
Vengeance has been targeted in recent months at numerous other allies, now regarded with more hostility by the White House than traditional adversaries such as Russia and China.

Annual joint military exercises with South Korea – a vital ally of Washington since the Korean war broke out in 1950 – were suddenly scaled down and cut short by six days last month, on Trump’s orders, because of his irritation that the Seoul government declined to join the fight against Iran.

He has repeatedly threatened to bomb or “blow up” the tiny Gulf kingdom of Oman, which has had friendly ties with the US for 200 years, if it impedes his efforts to reopen the strait of Hormuz, which Iran has closed to most commercial shipping.

The White House also announced the withdrawal of 5,000 US troops from Germany after the country’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, rebuffed pressure to get involved in the Iran conflict and said Trump had been “humiliated” in the conflict.
Threats of retribution have also been aimed at Spain, which has resisted pressure to boost defense spending, and Italy, whose prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, was a former Trump ally.
Turbulence under Trump

But Milei, a self-styled “anarcho-capitalist” who has paraded with a chainsaw to signify his attitude to public spending and attended Trump’s 2025 inauguration, remains on the US president’s good side.

Last year, the administration extended his troubled government a $20bn loan guarantee to stabilize the infamously shaky Argentinian economy – but premised the money on Milei’s party defeating the leftist opposition in forthcoming congressional elections, which it duly did.

This time there are no guarantees, other than that of never-ending turbulence at the hands of Trump. Such rough currents may be the “winds of change” Milei referenced in Thursday’s speech, delivered – Trump-style – with his cabinet members flanking him.

But he may have been aware the phrase had other, historical connotations – evoking the words of a famous speech in 1960 by then British prime minister Harold Macmillan in Cape Town, heralding independence for Britain’s former colonial possession in Africa.
“The wind of change is blowing through this continent,” Macmillan said then. “Whether we like it or not, this growth of national consciousness is a political fact.”

In his address, Milei suggested the sun was setting on Britain, just as it once did on its empire, citing multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. “It is clear that they are on a path of decline,” he pronounced.

He did not mention his own falling political popularity – a factor which may also have played a key role in the former military junta’s decision to seize the islands in 1982, as opposition grew against the backdrop of mass disappearances of political dissidents and multiple human rights abuses.

Then, too, Britain was grappling with tensions over immigration and race riots, soaring unemployment and long-term economic decline that Thatcher had been elected pledging to reverse. In the late winter of 1982, there was little sign that she was capable of doing so – until the Falklands conflict sparked a sudden upturn in her political fortunes.

But she had the solid backing of the special relationship, and her ideological soulmate, Ronald Reagan, in the White House. Andy Burnham, Britain’s newly installed Labour prime minister, must contend with the chill wind emanating from the menacing and destabilizing presence of Trump.

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte camp urges ICC to strengthen evidence verification
articles.summary: The camp of former President Rodrigo Duterte on Thursday asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) to amend its E-Court Protocol to strengthen verification requirements for open-source and…

blocks.text: Published September 5, 2026 4:13am

The camp of former President Rodrigo Duterte on Thursday asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) to amend its E-Court Protocol to strengthen verification requirements for open-source and user-generated material submitted as evidence.

In a submission before the ICC Trial Chamber III, the defense flagged several problems with the prosecution’s evidence, including illegible documents, audiovisual files without transcripts or translations, and pages from the same document being disclosed separately under different and nonconsecutive evidence reference numbers.

"Based on a small sample of documents from the same dataset which has already been received by the defense, it is clear that there are major issues with this collection of documents; it includes many duplicates and documents of very poor quality which, notwithstanding its volume, makes meaningful review immensely challenging," the defense said.
The defense said the prosecution had disclosed more than 25,000 evidence items as of the latest count, up from just over 5,000 items submitted before the confirmation hearing in February.
The prosecution has also signaled plans to submit another 200 gigabytes of material, the defense said.

"With three months until the start of trial, the defense is deeply concerned that the quality and quantity of the evidence in this case risks flooding the record with unreliable and/or irrelevant material. This would be detrimental for the parties and the Chamber’s search for the truth, and reputationally damaging for the Court," the defense said.

"This concern is particularly heightened in this case where, unlike in other cases previously before the Court, the parties and Chamber are operating in an environment where a huge volume of misinformation is being routinely created and shared online about these proceedings and the events on which they focus."
To mitigate this risk, the defense proposed adding an “Expert Verification” field to the E-Court Protocol for open-source and user-generated evidence.
The field would indicate whether an item submitted to the Court would be accompanied by an expert report.

"In the defense’s view, any such expert report ought to include, at a minimum, information on: the source of the item (both the sender/uploader and the creator of the piece of evidence, if known); its chain of custody and whether the item is the original or a copy; its metadata and any other technical aspects, such as the hash value generated at the time of capture; the steps taken to verify the material and to check for editing or manipulation," the defense said.

"It should also include information on the qualifications and experience of the person who undertook those steps to verify the material on behalf of the tendering party, and the methodology that they followed. Without this information, it would be very difficult for the Chamber to come to a view on the evidence’s relevance and admissibility, pursuant to Article 69(4) of the [Rome] Statute," it added.
It suggested that the Court approve a template for expert verification reports ahead of trial.

Duterte has been in ICC custody since March 2025 in connection with charges of crimes against humanity over killings during his tenure as Davao City mayor and in relation to the war on drugs during his presidency.
The trial is set to begin on November 30, 2026. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Billy Ray Cyrus reacts to Miley changing her stage name
articles.summary: Pop singer Miley dropped "Cyrus" from her name on her social media accounts earlier this week, and now her famous father Billy Ray Cyrus is clearing up the confusion on social media.

image.caption: Billy Ray Cyrus says his daughter dropping his last name and performing under the single name Miley is 'a natural progression for an iconic superstar legend.' (Ian Gavan/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment
Pop singer Miley dropped "Cyrus" from her name on her social media accounts earlier this week, and now her famous father Billy Ray Cyrus is clearing up the confusion on social media.
Country singer says 'family means more than ever now' in social media post
When pop singer Miley dropped the Cyrus from her name on her social media accounts earlier this week, tongues started wagging.
Was this the act of a distraught singer, mourning the loss of her honourary godmother, Dolly Parton?
Had she fallen out with her famous father, country singer Billy Ray Cyrus?
Or did it have something to do with the release of her upcoming album?
Billy Ray Cyrus is clearing up the confusion today with a post on social media.
"I always called my little girl Miley. Just … Miley, he wrote on Instagram, alongside a picture of him with his children when they were young.
Miley was named Destiny Hope Cyrus at birth, but as a baby she smiled so much, her father told Ellen DeGeneres, he started calling her Smiley — then Miley, and the name stuck.

Around this time, Billy Ray Cyrus also introduced his young daughter country music icon Dolly Parton, who he befriended while performing as her opening act on tour. He asked Parton to play the role of godmother to Miley.
Both Cyruses have publicly expressed how keenly they are feeling the loss of Parton, who died last week.
Billy Ray Cyrus, who turned 65 on the day of Parton's death, says family is more important him right now than ever before, and he doesn't begrudge his daughter performing under a single name.

"I told @miley yesterday I felt good about her going with her first name. I mentioned Dolly and Cher. Thinkin' about it more and more … Elvis ... Prince … and so on. It’s a natural progression for an iconic superstar legend."
This does not appear to be an official name change for Miley, merely a rebrand.
Her tenth studio album, BASS PERSUADES, is due to be released on Sept. 18, and she has also announced two concerts at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles in October.
"I’ve sat in those seats many times, but I’ve never taken the stage. L.A. is my heart and I’m bringing it home," she wrote this week on Instagram.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Helen Surgenor is a producer for CBC News based in Toronto, currently working for the entertainment unit. She spent years waking up before dawn to make the daily news podcast World Report. She has reported in Alberta, Iqaluit and Barbados. You can reach her at helen.surgenor@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Man charged with arson after cars torched outside Liberal MP's home
articles.summary: Toronto police say they have arrested and charged a man in connection to an arson investigation after several cars were torched at the home of a Scarborough MP last week.

image.caption: Roshvin Crofton, 24, is charged in connection with an alleged arson that happened outside a Liberal MP's home in Scarborough last week. (Toronto Police Service)

blocks.text: Toronto
Toronto police say they have arrested and charged a man in connection to an arson investigation after several cars were torched at the home of a Scarborough MP last week.
Scarborough Centre MP Salma Zahid's car and neighbouring vehicle torched last week
A man has been charged after several cars were torched at the home of a Scarborough MP last week, Toronto police say.

Roshvin Crofton, 24, was arrested Sunday. He is charged with arson causing damage to property, mischief over $5,000, conspiracy to commit an indictable offence, possession of incendiary material, and failure to comply with probation order, police said in a news release Friday.
A 2025 Hyundai Sonata, believed to be involved in the incident, was also seized. Police are looking for information on where the vehicle was in the days before the alleged arson.
Police say they are searching for a second suspect as well.
The alleged arson occurred in the driveway of Liberal MP Salma Zahid's home. Zahid represents the federal riding of Scarborough Centre-Don Valley East.
Video shows Liberal MP's car set on fire
Police say an "unknown suspect" approached the vehicles in the driveway early on Aug. 27, poured an accelerant on them and ignited two vehicles, causing them to catch fire, before fleeing the scene.
A third vehicle was damaged from the flames, police said.
Zahid welcomes arrest, says no word on motive
Zahid thanked Toronto police in a statement released Friday, shortly after they announced the arrest.
"I welcome word of an arrest and charges related to the arson incident outside my home on August 27th, and news the police are seeking an additional suspect in relation to this case," she said.
"As the investigation is ongoing, we still do not have information with regards to a motive for this incident."

Zahid, a Liberal backbencher, has been an MP for Scarborough Centre since 2015. She currently chairs the standing committee on science and research and is the vice-chair of the Canada-China legislative association.
The incident drew condemnation from numerous politicians, including Prime Minister Mark Carney.

articles.title: Outrage as Maltese tycoon acquitted in journalist's murder
articles.summary: Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech has been found not guilty of complicity to murder journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia. Almost nine years after the attack, the question of who ordered her death…

image.caption: Protesters gathered outside the Maltese Parliament following the verdict in the Caruana Galizia murder trial on WednesdayImage: Darrin Zammit Lupi/REUTERS

blocks.text: "Murderer!" — "Scum!" — "Mafia!"

As Yorgen Fenech left the courthouse in Valletta on Wednesday evening, he was confronted by the furious crowd outside. The 44-year-old Maltese businessman pushed through, flanked by his security guards. Just minutes earlier, a jury had acquitted him of ordering the murder of the 53-year-old investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.

The verdict came as a shock to her family. Her son, Matthew Caruana Galizia, said it was a "terrible decision by the jurors that our country may never recover from." He later doubled down on his criticism, describing the verdict in a post on Facebook as "obscene" and saying: "Their decision flies in the face of all evidence, of all logic, of the truth."

Almost nine years after Caruana Galizia's murder, Malta is again confronted with the crucial question: Who was responsible for her death on October 16, 2017? The men who procured the bomb, placed it under the driver's seat and detonated it remotely have already been convicted. But the person who contracted them to do it has still not been legally identified.

blocks.caption: Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech was acquitted on Wednesday of conspiracy and complicity to murderImage: Kevin Schembri Orland/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A difficult trial

For years, Fenech was considered to be the central figure in the investigations. His arrest on the morning of November 20, 2019, was like something out of a movie. His luxury yacht, Gio, had just left harbor when it was stopped by a Maltese military patrol boat. Fenech was arrested on board and subsequently interrogated by the police.

Fenech's arrest, and suspicion that people in government circles were involved in the crime, sparked protests all across the country. Joseph Muscat, prime minister at the time, was accused of protecting political allies and stepped down in January 2020. Fenech spent more than five years in detention before being released on bail, under strict conditions, in early 2025.
His trial only began this summer, and the final verdict was decisive. Eight of the nine jurors rejected the prosecution's argument that it was Fenech who had ordered the journalist's murder.
Who was responsible?

The prosecution case relied above all on the testimony of Melvin Theuma, who confessed to being the middleman and testified that Fenech had contracted him to organize the murder. Theuma received a pardon in exchange for his cooperation.
But Fenech's defense called Theuma's credibility into question, highlighting contradictions in his testimony and false statements he had made previously.

Fenech's lawyers also sought to prove that evidence pointing to Keith Schembri, chief of staff to Muscat at the time, was not properly followed up. Schembri has denied any involvement in the murder, and the investigators did not charge him as a suspect in this case.

blocks.caption: Investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed by a car bomb on October 16, 2017Image: Rene Rossignaud/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The public prosecutors' argument was that Caruana Galizia had been investigating Fenech, specifically his company 17 Black and the energy consortium ElectroGas, on suspicion of corruption. This, they said, meant Fenech had a motive for silencing her. She had not, however, been on the point of publishing anything that could have threatened him.
Open questions

Many in Malta are outraged by the not-guilty verdict. But there is no indication to date that Fenech did not receive a fair trial, or that the process was manipulated. For him to be convicted, Fenech's guilt had to be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

Caruana Galizia's family are therefore also focusing on institutional failures that they believe facilitated the murder. They complain that these have not been addressed, and necessary reforms not implemented. An official investigation already established, in 2021, that an "atmosphere of impunity" in Malta created conditions that made the murder possible.
Reforms in Malta

Since then, Malta has made progress with a series of reforms, but many say they do not go far enough. This is especially the case with regard to press freedom. In 2021, the committee of inquiry recommended that journalists be better protected against political and economic pressure and their role institutionally strengthened, yet the country is still waiting for comprehensive media reform.

Following years of discussion and a public consultation, the Maltese government brought the relevant bill before parliament in March 2026, but the legislation was not passed before early parliamentary elections in May.

In its latest Rule of Law Report, the European Commission only certifies limited progress made by Malta. It acknowledges that it has introduced some specific protection measures for journalists, but says core recommendations from the investigation into the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia remain unfulfilled.

blocks.caption: The European Commission has told Malta it needs to do more to strengthen official protections for journalists  Image: Sachelle Babbar/Zuma/picture alliance

blocks.text: Government sees progress

But the government paints a different picture. It has highlighted changes to the judiciary and anti-corruption measures, as well as better protection of journalistic sources, and additional measures to protect media professionals. This is what the EU Commission referred to as progress in specific areas.

The case has also shone a spotlight on the slow pace of the Maltese justice system. According to a report by the Daphne Caruana Galizia Foundation, 46% of homicide cases brought to trial between 2010 and 2020 had still not been concluded in mid-2025. The foundation regards this as a structural problem, and warns that when proceedings go on for so long, it compromises the chances of an effective prosecution.
Fresh investigation?

No decision has yet been made as to what will happen now, following Fenech's acquittal. Judge Edwina Grima has ordered that the evidence presented at trial be passed on to the chief of police, who will decide whether criminal proceedings should be brought against anyone else.
On Thursday, former PM Muscat said that, according to the public prosecutors, further investigations were ongoing.

blocks.caption: Nine years on, the person behind Daphne Caruana Galizia's murder has still not been brought to justice Image: AP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Institute of Maltese Journalists (IGM) has called on the authorities to pursue every line of inquiry that came to light during the trial — including, explicitly, those that lead to former high-ranking politicians. The acquittal must be respected as the outcome of the constitutional process, the IGM said, but it does not close the case.

The demonstrators outside the courthouse in Valletta are in no doubt. Someone must have issued a contract for the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia. And almost nine years after her death, still no one has been held responsible.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Yemen: Fighting intensifies amid Houthi push in the west
articles.summary: Houthi forces are trying to secure high ground and solidify their control of the entry to the Red Sea in the southwest. The Iran-backed militia abandoned a shaky truce with the Saudi-backed…

image.caption: A period of comparative calm in Yemen's 12-year civil war has been sundered amid the war with Iran [FILE: July 31, 2026]Image: Osamah Abdulrahman/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Both sides in Yemen's long-running civil war have sustained losses in a new push from the Houthi militia to try to seize control of the gateway to the Red Sea in the west.
The Iran-backed Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and much of the country, launched a ground offensive against the Saudi Arabia-led coalition supporting Yemen's government-in-exile on Thursday.

No casualty numbers were formally announced but news agencies citing sources off the record concurred that both sides had sustained dozens of losses, as well as civilians who were killed amid the fighting. The AFP news agency tallied 129 deaths as of Friday.
Officials also reported shelling and artillery fire forcing hundreds of families to flee from a pair of coastal cities, Hodeidah and Mokha, one held by either side in the conflict.
Why are the Houthis pushing to control this territory now?
Yemen has been in a state of civil war for almost exactly 12 years, and a period of comparative calm broke down this July amid the war with Iran in the Gulf.

The Houthis are targeting ports and elevated terrain held by Saudi-led forces that would improve their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, where the Red Sea meets the Gulf of Aden, leading out into the Arabian Sea and open waters.
Always a crucial waterway, its significance has increased amid the restrictions to traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
Houthis claim attacks on Saudi tankers in Red Sea

The Houthis declared a blockade on ships approaching the west coast of Saudi Arabia, with access to its eastern ports already impeded via Hormuz. But they are not ideally placed or equipped to enforce their stated desire.
Nevertheless they have already fired on several commercial vessels, causing severe damage and deaths in a few cases, even with their imperfect control of the relevant coastline.
What do we know about the intensified fighting?

Military sources speaking off the record told both the DPA and AFP news agencies that both sides had sustained multiple casualties. DPA put the figure in the dozens on both sides, AFP had a more precise estimate of roughly 60 on either side.
Exchanges of fire, on land as well as using rockets and drones, were reported in two southwestern provinces, Taiz and Hodeidah.

blocks.caption: Mokha also came under aerial bombardment last month but now the Houthis appear to be trying to approach it on landImage: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Houthis control the major western port of Hodeidah further north, but large chunks of Yemen's southwestern tip in Taiz including the port of Mokha near the strait are controlled by Saudi-led forces.
"They are going for Bab al-Mandeb," Mohammed al-Basha of the US-based risk advisory Basha Report told the AFP news agency.
Iran war: Analyzing the Houthi blockade against Saudi Arabia
Fighting for the high ground, for instance on Mount al-Numan overlooking Mokha, was particularly fierce.
"The Houthis feel that if they capture Bab al-Mandab or Mokha port they will be in a better position of power to negotiate with the government and the Saudis," al-Basha said.

articles.title: Saxony-Anhalt: Small parties will be the kingmakers
articles.summary: The far-right AfD has good odds of winning an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt's parliament this state election, enabling them to govern alone. It all depends on whether other parties make the cut.

image.caption: Saxony-Anhalt is governed from the state parliament in MagdeburgImage: ArTo/Zoonar/IMAGO

blocks.text: It's rare that a state parliament election in Germany attracts as much media interest as this one in Saxony-Anhalt. On September 6, 2026, the 1.7 million eligible voters in the eastern German state will decide whether the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party can form a state government for the first time.

So far, there has not been a head of government who belonged to a proven far-right party in post-World War II Germany — at neither federal nor state level. That would change if AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund were to be elected to this position, since the Office for the Protection of the Constitution in Saxony Anhalt already classified the AfD as such in 2023.
Siegmund's chances of a historical triumph are high: For months the AfD has been comfortably leading the polls with well over 40% of the vote.
AfD, CDU and Left Party will get into parliament

Aside from the AfD, there are only two other parties who can count on being included in the next state parliament: The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of current State Premier Sven Schulze and the socialist Left Party, which is traditionally strong in eastern Germany, the former socialist GDR.
All other parties have cause for concern they could fail to reach the 5% threshold of votes necessary for entry into parliaments in Germany.
This even applies to the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), who currently form part of the federal government coalition with the CDU and its Bavarian counterpart, the Christian Social Union (CSU).
SPD, Greens, FDP, BSW might not make the 5% mark
The SPD is losing popularity nationwide. In Saxony-Anhalt, they are polling below the 8% they won five years ago.

The third party in Saxony-Anhalt's current governing coalition, formed in 2021, has even fewer hopes: The neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP) are polling only about 3%. Following the FDP's failure in the Bundestag general election of 2025 and multiple defeats at the state level, supporters are bracing themselves for the next setback.

The environmentalist Greens are also concerned about returning to the state parliament. The party, whose core voter base is in wealthy western German cities, is vehemently rejected by many voters in rural areas because of its climate policies and multicultural vision of society.
Concern over Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW)

And then there is the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), founded in 2024 by its namesake, a former Left Party co-leader. The party is economically left-leaning, but socially right-wing conservative and populist. This is its first time participating in a state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

After the BSW gained 6.2% of the vote in the European parliament elections in 2024 and won results of between about 12% and 16% in the eastern German states of Brandenburg, Saxony and Thuringia during its first year, it failed by only a few thousand votes to reach the 5% hurdle to enter German parliament in the 2025 general election.

The BSW never really recovered from this setback. They went on to be defeated in three further state parliament elections. The party also has cause for concern in Saxony-Anhalt, where it has been polling under 5%.

Should it win representation after all, Sahra Wagenknecht has already announced that her party's lawmakers would not vote an AfD premier into office, but abstain from the vote paving the way for him to win a majority in parliament and take office.
Considering the poor polling numbers for the BSW in Saxony-Anhalt, political scientist Oliver Lembcke speaks of an "endgame" for the party as a whole.
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?
Small parties could prevent absolute majority for the AfD
The fact is: The more parties fail to reach the threshold, the higher the likelihood of the Alternative for Germany will be able to govern alone.

On the other hand, if aside from the AfD, the CDU, Left Party and SPD win representation in the next Saxony-Anhalt parliament, and those three parties together hold more seats than the AfD, the situation is complicated. This is because in 2018 the CDU adopted a so-called "resolution of incompatibility," which rejects cooperation with both the AfD and the Left Party.
If the CDU sticks to this, forming even a minority government would be very difficult, perhaps impossible.
Could the CDU form a minority government?

Political scientist Lembcke from Ruhr University Bochum in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia argues that the CDU should have adapted its incompatibility resolution to the changed conditions of the party systems and political landscape. Because it has failed to do so, this issue could now escalate drastically in Saxony-Anhalt.
The Left Party is prepared to support Premier Sven Schulze of the CDU to secure a second term.

"In recent years, we, the Left Party, have shown that we take responsibility for this country. Especially when it comes to inhibiting the AfD," Left Party co-leader Luigi Pantisano told television broadcaster ZDF.
He pointed to the states of Thuringia and Saxony, where the CDU leads coalition governments without a parliamentary majority and depends on the support of the Left Party.

Given the foreseeably complicated situation, one thing is clear ahead of the September 6 election: either Saxony-Anhalt faces an incredibly difficult coalition-building process, or the state will be governed by the AfD — if the party profits from the failure of many small parties and thereby receives an absolute majority in the state parliament.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Ex-MILF military spox questions presence of guns in group’s assembly
articles.summary: COTABATO CITY, BARMM, Philippines — A former official of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) on Friday slammed the erstwhile rebel group for allegedly violating the election gun ban imposed by…

blocks.text: COTABATO CITY, BARMM, Philippines — A former official of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) on Friday slammed the erstwhile rebel group for allegedly violating the election gun ban imposed by the Commission on Elections (Comelec) when heavily armed members of the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces (BIAF) showed up during its gathering in Sultan Kudarat, Maguindanao del Norte on Thursday, Sept. 3.
The BIAF is the MILF’s military wing that is set for decommissioning in keeping with the 2014 peace deal.

Abunawas Maslamama, who used to be BIAF spokesperson under the pseudonym Von Al Haq, said the open display and carrying of firearms during the BIAF Grand Assembly at the MILF headquarters in Camp Darapanan was a violation of the election gun ban that has been in effect for the Bangsamoro parliamentary elections.
“They were in full battle gear, brandishing firearms as shown on social media and during live streaming of the front’s assembly,” Maslamama said in a social media post.
Maslamama was also the BIAF intelligence chief before he was removed from the post on Thursday.
He also lambasted the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP), the MILF’s regional political party, for joining the BIAF assembly and turned the event as a political rally.

“This is an MILF event and it happened inside the MILF camp so there was no violation of election gun ban, no violation of ceasefire agreement,” a BIAF commander said in another social media post in response to Maslamama’s claim.

Maslamama, who also served as senior minister of BARMM when MILF Chief Al Haj Murad Ebrahim was the chief minister, urged the Comelec to issue clarification on the concerns he aired to avoid confusion as the elections draw near.
Maslamama left UBJP and joined the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP), now headed by Bangsamoro interim Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua. /cb

articles.title: Woman robbed, shot while heading home from bank in Cotabato
articles.summary: COTABATO CITY, BARMM, Philippines — A woman lost P135,000 in cash to suspected robbers who attacked her in Barangay Rosary Heights 2 here on Friday afternoon, Sept. 4, despite an election gun ban.…

blocks.text: COTABATO CITY, BARMM, Philippines — A woman lost P135,000 in cash to suspected robbers who attacked her in Barangay Rosary Heights 2 here on Friday afternoon, Sept. 4, despite an election gun ban.

Colonel Jibin Bongcayao, Cotabato City police director, said that the woman, identified only as “Mercy,” withdrew cash from a local bank and boarded a “habal-habal” on her way home when the suspects followed her.
As the “habal-habal” reached Climente Alino Street in Barangay Rosary Heights 2 at 3:10 p.m., one of the suspects grabbed the victim’s sling bag that contained the money.
She resisted but the suspects shot her in the face. The bullet also hit the habal-habal driver in his neck.
The suspect fled toward Notre Dame Avenue, also in Barangay Rosary Heights 2, and made good their escape with their loot.
The woman and the motorbike driver were rushed to Cotabato Regional and Medical Center where they are now recuperating.
Police found empty shells for caliber .45 pistol at the crime scene.
The attack occurred amid the tight implementation of an election gun ban as part of preparations for the Bangsamoro parliamentary elections on Sept. 14. /cb

articles.title: Cops bust illegal mining activity in Misamis Oriental
articles.summary: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY, Philippines — A suspected illegal small-scale mining operation in Misamis Oriental ground to a halt late Wednesday afternoon, Sept. 2, after security forces caught the operator…

blocks.text: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY, Philippines — A suspected illegal small-scale mining operation in Misamis Oriental ground to a halt late Wednesday afternoon, Sept. 2, after security forces caught the operator red-handed processing mineral ore without permits in the hinterland village of Limonda of Opol town.

Joint government troops and police units swooped down on the site in Zone 2 at around 5:20 p.m., seizing an estimated P280,000 worth of mineral ore and arresting a 29-year-old local resident identified only as “Gil.”

The operatives—composed of the Opol Municipal Police Station, the 2nd Provincial Mobile Force Company of Misamis Oriental, the Regional Mobile Force Battalion 10, the Philippine Army’s 88th Infantry Battalion, Task Force Opol, and Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB)-deputized personnel from Task Force Kalikasan ug Kalinaw—caught the suspect in the act of running ball mill drums.

When asked by authorities to present the necessary permits authorizing the operation, the suspect failed to provide any valid documents. He was arrested on the spot and informed of his constitutional rights.
Authorities confiscated 10 ball mill drums containing 16 bags of unfinished milled ore.
The suspect is currently detained at the Opol Municipal Police Station, where he faces charges for violating the Philippine Mining Act of 1995 (RA 7942).

The seized mineral ore was taken to the police station for documentation and proper disposition, while the 10 ball mill drums were placed under the temporary custody of the Barangay Limonda council pending turnover to the MGB.
Brig. Gen. Nestor Babagay Jr., Police Regional Office 10 director, said the operation underscores the police force’s drive to halt environmental destruction in Northern Mindanao.
“This operation sends a clear message: illegal mining will not be tolerated,” Babagay said. /cb

articles.title: Germany's alliance against the far right
articles.summary: Trade unions, churches and human rights activists are worried about the rise of the far-right AfD. How can civil society protect people who are threatened by far-right extremism?

image.caption: In 2024, hundreds of thousands across the country rallied in protest against right-wing extremismImage: Stefan Boness/IPON/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fighting for democracy and human rights in Germany today means mustering up a lot of courage. For Felix Pankonin, locking and checking all doors and windows around the house has become practically second nature. Sometimes a hot-tempered lawmaker from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party shows up on his property; his bicycles have been vandalized; and other times he receives threats that something will happen to his animals. Most recently, his partner was physically assaulted.
Pankonin is the project director of educational programs on political issues, Jewish history and antisemitism at the Hillersche Villa in Zittau, in the eastern German state of Saxony.

The situation is similar for Keerthana Kuperan, who works as a political advisor at DaMOst, the umbrella organization for migrant groups in eastern Germany. Yes, says Kuperan, whose parents are from Sri Lanka, right-wing extremism has had a major impact on her work over the past three years.
"We have completely different security protocols now. After 6:00 p.m., no one is left alone in the office, and when putting up posters in rural areas, security measures are put in place beforehand."

Her work is primarily focused on ensuring the safety of activists. Another aspect of her work involves dealing with challenges from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which files parliamentary information requests, often on migration, in order to delay political proceedings and highlight issues that should not really be controversial.

blocks.caption: Ahead of the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, numerous business owners with a background of migration went on strike against racism and fascism, and in support of a free and democratic societyImage: Peter Gercke/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Saxony-Anhalt, a federal state with a very low proportion of foreigners, state legislative elections will be held on September 6. DaMOst observes that the political landscape has shifted to the right. This has led to the discrediting of democratic networks, which has affected their funding and job opportunities.
Green Party politician becomes target of hostilities

Miriam Zeller, a councilwoman in Stendal (a city of 37,000 in Saxony-Anhalt), is a member of the environmentalist Green Party and is running in the state election on September 6. Zeller told DW that the hostility was even more intense when the Greens were in power.

Her daughter stopped being invited to birthday parties, and she herself was viciously accused of being a warmonger. From the very beginning, the Greens had declared their solidarity with Ukraine after it had come under attack from Russia.
"It can't get any worse than this," says Zeller.
However, she pointed out that, fortunately, as a teacher, she is a civil servant and therefore cannot lose her job.
For others, the specter of losing one's job — should the AfD come to power — is very real.

blocks.caption: Miriam Zeller, a Green Party candidate, is feeling the impact of the shift to the right in her private life as wellImage: Miriam Zeller

blocks.text: Alliance for Democracy: Educating people on how to defend themselves

People like Pankonin, Kuperan and Zeller need more protection. The Together for Democracy alliance aims to support individuals or institutions that are being attacked or threatened by far-right extremists.

The aim of the group's Solidarity Agreement — which over 80 groups have signed, including labor unions, the major Christian churches, sports organizations, human rights groups as well as social and environmental organizations — is to ensure that anyone who is targeted for their commitment to democracy will not be left alone. The groups joined forces in 2024 to form an alliance against the far right when it became clear that attacks on democracy were intensifying.

Now, alliance members want to also offer help and support in the event of attacks on youth or cultural centers, hate campaigns against people who speak out publicly, or when volunteers are threatened — whether through public expressions of solidarity or by providing legal or financial support. The alliance includes powerful actors such as the German Trade Union Federation (DGB) and environmental organizations like Greenpeace.

Yasmin Fahimi, the head of the DGB, which has over five million members, took the opportunity to present the new agreement in Berlin. When asked by DW whether the AfD, in the event of an election victory, could actually fire all public employees, Fahimi was clear.

"This fantasy of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt — to carry out a complete personnel shake-up in government agencies, ministries, courts and the police — is completely unlawful," Fahimi said. "We are making it clear to our members that they can fight back against this. It is also a manifestation of an authoritarian mindset to believe that one can simply issue a decree and do as one pleases. That's not how our democracy works."

That is why the DGB is training its members both in constitutional law and civil service law so they can defend themselves, Fahimi said. The trade union leader calls for more commitment from politicians.

"We must ensure — especially in regional areas, but also within our institutions — that people cannot simply be forced to comply with unlawful orders. I believe it would be good for the Conference of Interior Ministers to discuss how to provide clear information, seminars and workshops on these issues, so that public servants, ministry employees and staff at institutions governed by the rule of law are not left to fend for themselves," Fahimi told DW.
Threats, abuse to German mayors hurting local government
Hope for help for queer people following the Berlin attack

"Of course, this alliance can mean more protection for queer people who are active on the ground," says Andre Lehmann, from the Queer Diversity Association(LSVD+) — a civil rights organization that has represented the interests and concerns of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans* and intersex queer people (LGBTQ+) since 1990.

"Right now, we're seeing a lot of attacks on Pride events all over Germany. In some cases, local organizers don't even know what to do in such situations. That's where an alliance like this can step in," Lehmann said in an interview with DW.
The Islamist attack on the Pride event in Berlinhas deeply unsettled the queer community, said Lehmann. On top of that, many democracy projects are being financially bled dry right now of all times.

The alliance will hardly be able to make up for the lack of funding for democracy projects that has resulted from the federal government's cuts and restructuring. However, teaming up with other organizations helps build strength, says Sophie Lampl, who works for Greenpeace.

"That is certainly one of the strengths we can bring as an environmental organization: our ability to campaign. To provide support when civil society organizations or individuals are attacked, to publicly stand up for them and to bring this injustice to light," Lampl argues.
Will the alliance also be able to help in rural areas?

Felix Pankonin has often helped the Together for Democracy alliance — by providing legal advice, funding for security and moral support. Pankonin would like to see more involvement from major organizations in rural areas.

Green Party politician Miriam Zeller reports that she has also received aid from small local networks. She believes that a large network, with its newfound solidarity, can make a big difference and could be a vital source of support, even in rural areas.
Andre Lehmann sounds determined: "We will defend our democracy and, if necessary, guide our local people through this valley," he says.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Romualdez’s lawyer says Bonoan drop from plunder case ‘alarming’
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The dropping of plunder charges against former Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan is alarming as it appears he is being prepared as a potential witness against Leyte Rep.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The dropping of plunder charges against former Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan is alarming as it appears he is being prepared as a potential witness against Leyte Rep. Ferdinand Martin Romualdez despite the absence of an initial testimony, the lawmaker’s lawyer said on Friday.

In a statement, Fajardo reiterated that Bonoan never mentioned anything about Romualdez being involved in the alleged budget insertions in the 2025 national budget and the anomalous infrastructure projects—from the congressional inquiries and the investigation done by the Independent Commission for Infrastructure (ICI).

“Nang magsimula itong reklamo ng special panel against Congressman Romualdez, wala pong anumang salaysay doon, wala po man lang kahit ni isang taga-DPWH, ni isang statement from Secretary Bonoan, kahit doon sa Blue Ribbon Committee, kahit doon sa Independent Commission for Infrastructure, wala pong nag-uugnay kay Congressman Romualdez,” Fajardo said.

(When this complaint was initiated by the special panel against Congressman Romualdez, there was no statement there, not even one statement from a DPWH personnel or Secretary Bonoan, even during the Blue Ribbon Committee or at the Independent Commission for Infrastructure, there is nothing that links to Congressman Romualdez.)

“Ibig sabihin, wala silang makita na partikular na DPWH project kung saan nag-participate o allegedly nag-impluwensiya si Congressman Romualdez para maapektuhan ang resulta, para manalo ang isang partikular na contractor. Walang ganung alegasyon kaya nakakagulat na si Secretary Bonoan all of a sudden is now available as a potential witness,” he added.

(This means they cannot see anything particular to a DPWH project where Congressman Romualdez participated or allegedly influenced the bidding process to favor a specific contractor. There is no such allegation; that’s why it is surprising that Secretary Bonoan all of a sudden is now available as a potential witness.)
Fajardo said that this background makes the Sandiganbayan’s decision to drop the plunder raps and release Bonoan alarming and shocking.
“Iyang naging desisyon po ay alarming at nakakagulat, ‘yan po ay nakakabahala,” Fajardo said.
(That decision is alarming and shocking, it raises concerns.)
“And then suddenly, malaya na siya at granted ang immunity practically kasi hindi na siya akusado,” he added.
(And then suddenly, he is free and granted immunity practically because he is no longer an accused.)

On Thursday, the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division ordered Bonoan’s release, recalling an order to commit Bonoan to hospital arrest at the Philippine National Police General Hospital (PNPGH) in Camp Crame.
Bonoan had been under hospital arrest since June 2026 at the PNPGH in Camp Crame due to several illnesses.
The Fifth Division’s move means that it has granted a motion made orally by Bonoan’s lawyer Stefanie Ong, during the hearing on Thursday.

This came two days after the court granted a motion by state prosecutors to exclude Bonoan from the graft and plunder charges against him, Senator Jinggoy Estrada, and three former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) district engineers.

This is not the first time that Romualdez’s camp has made accusations about Bonoan being forced to produce evidence against the lawmaker, who was Speaker of the House during the 19th Congress and the early part of the 20th Congress.

Last August 6, Fajardo said they believe Bonoan really has nothing to say but is being placed in a precarious position when investigators suddenly claim that the former DPWH chief will be a key witness against Romualdez.

Fajardo did not mention who thought of having Bonoan as a state witness, but last June 30, Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano admitted that the decision to tap the former secretary as state witness was made in order to strengthen their case against Romualdez.
Prior to his, Fajardo said Bonoan may be under pressure to testify regarding the infrastructure corruption scandal when a transfer to an ordinary jail facility was looming.

Romualdez has been accused of facilitating budget insertions to implement anomalous infrastructure programs and receiving kickbacks from these projects. However, the lawmaker and his legal team have insisted that he is not involved in any wrongdoing, saying several times that as Speaker, he does not have control over every step of the budget-making process in Congress.

Eventually, several witnesses like Orly Guteza and some of the 18 former security aides of ex-Ako Bicol party-list Rep. Elizaldy Co—who initially claimed that they were involved in a money-delivery scheme—recanted their statements.

For Guteza, he claimed that it was the idea of Senator Rodante Marcoleta and former Anakalusugan party-list Rep. Mike Defensor to fabricate a story, saying in an affidavit dated August 13 that he had no personal knowledge of the alleged delivery of “maleta” (suitcases) containing cash at Co’s Pasig residence, as well as the alleged delivery to Romualdez’s residence in Taguig.
Early this August, four of the 18 former Co bodyguards claimed in a report aired by GMA’s 24 Oras that they signed the joint affidavit because they had allegedly been promised financial assistance.

They were referring to the affidavit that they signed and presented during a February 24, 2026 press briefing along with Baligod, who was their lawyer. The 18 bodyguards made the same claims as Guteza—claiming that they were involved in the delivery of cash from Co to different lawmakers.

Romualdez used these recantations to bolster his claim that the charges against him should be dropped. Last August 20, Romualdez’s camp submitted a supplemental counter affidavit to the Office of the Ombudsman, citing the recantations and the sworn statements of 25 of Co’s former drivers and security aides as reasons to junk the complaints against him.

Furthermore, the supplemental counter-affidavit that Romualdez submitted stated that some of Co’s 25 former security aides were initially asked by lawyer Levito Baligod to join the cause of the ‘18 bodyguards’ in exchange for financial benefit. /cb

articles.title: Sherwin Gatchalian flags 488 HFEP infrastructure implementation deficiencies
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Friday flagged 488 infrastructure implementation deficiencies under the Department of Health"s (DOH) Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP).

blocks.text: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Friday flagged 488 infrastructure implementation deficiencies under the Department of Health’s (DOH) Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP).
Gatchalian raised the concern during the DOH’s 2027 budget briefing at the Senate, noting that the figures were documented before DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado assumed office.

“Merong 38 projects worth P11 billion na delayed in implementation. Merong 136 projects worth P1.1 billion [na] idle, unutilized, [or] non-operational. Meron P1.1 billion underutilized… Merong 227 [projects] worth P3.1 billion unimplemented/not yet started,” Gatchalian said.

(There are 38 projects worth P11 billion that are delayed in implementation. There are 136 projects worth P1.1 billion that are idle, unutilized, or non-operational. There is P1.1 billion underutilized… And there are 227 projects worth P3.1 billion that are unimplemented or have not yet started.)

Gatchalian asked the DOH how it plans to address these deficiencies, considering that the government has already allocated P17.27 billion for the projects and is set to allocate another P14.5 billion under the 2027 national budget.
Mercado said the DOH is looking to improve allocative efficiency to ensure that the appropriate types and standards of health facilities are built and operated based on local needs.

“Ang plano ko po ay mag-define ano ba talaga ang basic standard of a typical RHU (Rural Health Unit), then ano po yung next level? Kailangan ba per district ay meron isang Super Health Center (SHCS)? And then going up, in the province, should district hospitals be standardized para may standard din po for district hospitals of such a big geographic catchment should contain these equipment,” Mercado explained.

(My plan is to define the basic standard of a typical Rural Health Unit (RHU), and then determine the next level. Does every district need a Super Health Center (SHC)? Moving up to the provincial level, should district hospitals be standardized so that facilities serving large geographic catchment areas contain the appropriate equipment?)
“Allocative efficiency po, Sen., para alam natin. Kasi nga po ngayon when I looked at the HFEP—tabi-tabi, gusto kanya-kanyang MR, CT scan, na hindi naman po ganong ka-efficient,” he added.

(This is about allocative efficiency, Senator, so we have clear guidelines. Right now, when I look at the HFEP, facilities are built side by side, with each one wanting its own MRI or CT scan, which isn't very efficient.)
Regarding physical infrastructure, Mercado said the agency plans to prioritize completing facilities that have already been constructed but remain non-operational.

“Looking at existing facilities, I believe our priority should be finishing those that are completed but non-operational—perhaps they just lack equipment—or those that are partially completed but operating, which might just need facility completion. For those that are partially completed and non-operating, we need to check if they lack manpower,” Mercado explained in a mix of Filipino and English.
Mercado said the DOH would also verify whether site conditions comply with the specific requirements of the requested healthcare facilities.

The low operational rate of Super Health Centers (SHCs) was also highlighted during the deliberations, with Gatchalian noting that only 244 of 820 planned facilities have been completed and are operational.
“Nakita ko na isa rin sa mga problema 'yung Super Health Centers no na ang daming unused,” Gatchalian said.
(I noticed that one of the recurring issues involves the Super Health Centers, many of which remain unused.)
“About P2.9 billion completed but not operational. About P3.9 billion not completed or no clear status update, meaning di alam kung anong situation na,” he added.
(About P2.9 billion worth are completed but non-operational. Around P3.9 billion worth are incomplete or have no clear status updates, meaning their current situation is unknown.)
Given the concerns raised, the Senate President urged the DOH to consider alternative measures to efficiently implement pending projects.
Gatchalian said construction delays remain a chronic government problem, affecting not only the DOH but also several other agencies.
Before Mercado could respond, Senator Panfilo Lacson interjected, pointing out that major project delays and fund underutilization often stem from congressional insertions.

He explained that some projects included in the General Appropriations Act end up unimplemented because they were not part of the DOH’s original program and were instead inserted by lawmakers during the budget process.
“Ang major cause ng delay at tsaka yung mga underutilization ng pondo, insertions di ba? So hindi kasalanan ng DOH kasi ito yung post-NEP,” Lacson said.
(The primary cause of delays and underutilized funds is insertions, isn't it? So it isn't entirely the DOH's fault because these occur after the National Expenditure Program (NEP).)
“Meron kayong programa sa NEP, hindi niya ma-execute properly kasi hindi kasama sa plano ninyo because of insertions made by legislators. Huwag na kayo mahiya, 'yan naman ang totoo di ba?” he added.

(You have your program under the National Expenditure Program, but you can't execute it properly because it wasn't part of your original plan due to legislative insertions. Don't be shy to admit it—that's the truth, right?)
Mercado responded to Lacson, saying, “Partly.”

Building on Lacson’s point, Gatchalian added that the non-operational status of many SHCs also results from a failure to assess whether local government units (LGUs) have the capacity to operate the facilities before they are constructed.

“Ito, konektado sa sinabi ni Sen. Ping na marami rin kasing mga nai-insert na Super Health Center, ayaw naman patakbuhin ng LGU dahil ayaw nilang magbayad ng kuryente, hindi sila makakuha ng nurse, ayaw nila bumili ng gamot,” Gatchalian said.

(This connects to what Sen. Ping mentioned about many Super Health Centers being inserted. The LGUs don't want to run them because they don't want to pay for electricity, they can't hire nurses, or they refuse to procure medicine.)
“So in other words, nakatayo na yung Super Health Center, ayaw angkinin ng LGU so nagiging problema rin,” he added.
(So in other words, the Super Health Center gets built, but the LGU refuses to assume responsibility for it, which creates another problem.)

Mercado confirmed that he had encountered governors who were surprised to find health facilities being constructed in their jurisdictions even though the projects were not included in their Provincial Health Investment Plans. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Mayon records 2nd-highest sulfur dioxide emission since July
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Mayon Volcano recorded its second-highest sulfur dioxide (SO2) emission since volcanic gas concentrations began declining in July, prompting state seismologists on Friday to…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Mayon Volcano recorded its second-highest sulfur dioxide (SO2) emission since volcanic gas concentrations began declining in July, prompting state seismologists on Friday to warn of the possibility of renewed eruptive unrest.

In an advisory, the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (Phivolcs) said SO2 emissions from Mayon’s summit crater reached 8,165 tonnes per day on Thursday, based on averaged measurements from stationary ultraviolet spectrometry.
This was significantly higher than the volcano’s average SO2 emission of 4,196 tonnes per day since its alert status was lowered to Alert Level 2 on Aug. 5.
The increase was accompanied by a slight rise in low-frequency volcanic earthquakes (LFVQs), which Phivolcs attributed to volcanic degassing.
As of noon this Friday, four LFVQs had been recorded by the Mayon Volcano Network, although real-time seismic energy release remained at background levels.
Phivolcs also noted a short-term swelling or pressurization trend in the northern and eastern sectors of Mayon’s edifice based on readings from electronic tilt deformation stations.
“Nonetheless, elevated volcanic SO2 emissions could forewarn of a potential shift to renewed eruptive activity at the summit crater,” Phivolcs said.

The agency warned that a renewed eruption could generate life-threatening hazards, including pyroclastic density currents or uson, rockfalls, ballistic fragments, and extensive ashfall that could affect communities downwind of the volcano.
Mayon remains under Alert Level 2, indicating a moderate level of unrest, but Phivolcs said there are new possibilities of eruptive unrest recurring.
The public was reminded to stay out of the six-kilometer Permanent Danger Zone around the volcano.
Communities and local governments within areas identified as vulnerable to pyroclastic density currents were also urged to prepare for a possible escalation to Alert Level 3.
Phivolcs also advised increased vigilance against lahars and sediment-laden streamflows along channels draining the volcano, particularly during sustained heavy or intense rainfall.

Civil aviation authorities were likewise urged to advise pilots to avoid flying close to Mayon’s summit, as ash and ballistic fragments from a sudden eruption could pose hazards to aircraft. —RENDELL IVAN MANUEL, INQUIRER.NET TRAINEE

articles.title: Cambridge University probing conduct of academic suspended by Reform UK
articles.summary:
James Orr, an associate professor, was shown in Channel 4 News footage apparently trying to sidestep electoral law

Cambridge University has said it is examining the conduct of James Orr, its…

blocks.text: Cambridge University has said it is examining the conduct of James Orr, its associate professor and a top Reform UK aide, after he was filmed appearing to try to circumvent electoral laws on foreign political donations.

Orr, the suspended head of policy for the party, is one of two senior officials to step aside after claims that he orchestrated a plot to have polling paid for by a foreign firm – something that is impermissible under British electoral law.
The academic was filmed by a group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, seemingly attempting to sidestep election laws.
In a statement shared with the Guardian, a spokesperson for the University of Cambridge said: “The university is looking into these matters.”
Orr is an associate professor of religion at Cambridge’s divinity faculty and teaches students at the university.
Little known outside UK and US political circles, Orr has been a highly influential intellectual force within Reform. He was labelled the party’s “philosopher king” by news organisation Politico.

A key attraction for senior figures within Reform when appointing Orr was his high-level US political contacts within the Maga movement. JD Vance, the US vice-president has called him his “intellectual mentor” and his “British Sherpa”.
Footage broadcast by Channel 4 News on Thursday night showed an undercover reporter posing as a UK-based supporter in conversation with Orr.
Orr discussed commissioning polling that was secretly organised by Reform, but suggested it be paid for by a US company belonging to the fake supporter’s supposed father.
In a separate clip, Orr can be heard saying of the poll funding arrangement that Farage “doesn’t know, won’t know” and it was the kind of thing he would “rather not know”.
Reform UK initially described the Channel 4 and Verbatim investigation as a “hoax”.
On Thursday evening, Orr posted a video on his X account in which he said: “There is absolutely no way this could amount to a benefit or donation in kind at all.”
He also dismissed Verbatim as “politically motivated actors trying to discredit a political opponent through dubious legal means”.

Still, on Friday morning, both he and senior aide to Nigel Farage, Dan Jukes – who has also denied wrongdoing – stood down pending an internal party investigation into the claims raised by the broadcast.
Farage, who was also featured in the investigation meeting with the fake supporters, further distanced himself from Orr and Jukes on Friday.
The party leader told reporters: “The two individuals involved are not even part of our fundraising team, so they should have gone through the appropriate channels.
“Checks would have been made and they would never, ever have got to sit down at a table with me.”
The Guardian has approached Orr for comment.

articles.title: Cambridge University asks former chief crown prosecutor to open Arday review
articles.summary:
Nazir Afzal to focus in review’s first stage on support given to professor in immediate period before his death

The University of Cambridge has asked Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown…

blocks.text: The University of Cambridge has asked Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, to lead the first part of its review into the death of the scholar Jason Arday.

Arday died at his home in south London on 14 August, nine days after his resignation as a Cambridge professor amid swirling allegations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career.

Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, said the time since Arday’s death had been “a period of profound sadness and reflection” for the university, and sought to defend her institution from criticism.

“We worked very hard to support Professor Arday during an appalling period of external criticism and focus but given the devastating outcome, we are all asking ourselves whether we could have and should have done more. This review will answer that question.
“We are committed to ensuring that any recommendations arising from the review are addressed and adopted with clear accountability for delivering necessary changes,” Prentice said.

blocks.caption: Jason Arday was found dead at home in south London on 14 August. Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian

blocks.text: Arday was named professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, with the university highlighting his appointment as the university’s youngest-ever black professor at the age of 37.

Arday denied the accusations of plagiarism levelled against him but on 5 August the university said it would hold an investigation into his academic qualifications. Arday resigned hours after the investigation was announced.
Prentice said the review would be in two parts, with the first, led by Afzal, to focus on the support given to Arday in the immediate period before his death.

Afzal said: “I am honoured to have been asked to lead part one of this important independent review. At its heart is a person, a family and a community who have been profoundly affected by Professor Arday’s death. It is important that we approach this work with both rigour and humanity.

“My responsibility will be to listen carefully, examine the evidence thoroughly and understand what support, interventions and protections were available to Professor Arday in the period before his death. We must be willing to ask difficult questions, including whether more could and should have been done.
“This work will be conducted independently and with urgency.”

Afzal, a University of Birmingham graduate, is the chancellor of the University of Manchester, after a career as head of the CPS in the north-west of England, during which he prosecuted child exploitation rings in Rochdale. In 2022 he led an independent review into London fire brigade that exposed a culture of misogyny, racism and bullying.
after newsletter promotion

Prentice said: “I am very grateful to Nazir for agreeing to lead this part of the review. He is a highly respected legal professional who will ask challenging questions about the support that was offered to Professor Arday during his time at Cambridge.”

The university said the review’s second stage would consider “the wider context of Professor Arday’s time at the university”, including the recruitment of senior academic staff, the university’s response to allegations of research misconduct, and the support it gave to academics “subject to extraordinary public and media scrutiny”.
Cambridge said it would appoint an independent external chair for the second part and an expert panel “including individuals with lived experience” to advise the review.
It said part one of the review was expected to report within three months, and the second part within six months of establishing the expert panel.

Earlier this week, Jacqui Smith, the minister responsible for higher education, told parliament that she was “more than just keeping an eye” on Cambridge’s response to Arday’s death. Smith said that England’s higher education regulator, the Office for Students, had the powers to investigate further if necessary.

articles.title: Farage seeks to shore up damaged leadership as scandal engulfs Reform conference
articles.summary:
Splits emerge within party after resignation of officials reported to police for apparent plot to evade donations law

Nigel Farage sought to shore up his damaged leadership on Friday as he…
articles.byline: Rowena Mason, Ben Quinn and Pippa Crerar

blocks.text: Nigel Farage sought to shore up his damaged leadership on Friday as he attempted to distance himself from two of his most senior officials reported to the police for apparently plotting to evade the law on foreign donations.

As the scandal engulfed Reform UK’s party conference in Birmingham, Farage was forced to suspend his closest aide, Dan Jukes, and head of policy, James Orr, after an undercover investigation by reporters from a group called Verbatim.

He later acknowledged Jukes and Orr had made “human error” and were “not authorised” to act in the way they did when trying to orchestrate donations to benefit the party from a fake US businessman, who was not permitted to give money.

blocks.caption: Dan Jukes, left, speaks to Nigel Farage before an interview in Clacton-on-Sea in July 2024. Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters

blocks.text: The Met police are now assessing the evidence after a complaint that Farage, Orr and Jukes may have broken political funding laws, with sources suggesting a full investigation is highly likely to be launched. They all deny wrongdoing.

Orr is an associate professor of divinity at the University of Cambridge who had been working for Reform, reporting directly to Farage, since February. In relation to the undercover footage of Orr, a spokesperson for the university said Cambridge was “looking into these matters”. Jukes is Farage’s closest aide who has been at his side for more than a decade working on communications and strategy.

Farage had been introduced by Jukes to the would-be donor from the US promising to give £500,000 despite not being eligible, who was really an undercover reporter. The Reform leader then appeared to endorse the scheme for the impermissible US donor to give money through his son, a UK intermediary, by saying “thank you, both” and “all above board”.

blocks.caption: James Orr, right, takes part in a Turning Point USA debate in December last year. Photograph: Caitlin O’Hara/Reuters

blocks.text: After dismissing the sting as a “hoax”, Reform began an organised campaign to limit the damage to Farage personally before his main conference speech, after a summer of scandals over his finances including an undeclared gift of £5m.

Addressing the allegations, the Reform leader responded by reading out a legal statement in which he dismissed the allegations as “a little local difficulty” and described the reports as “an exercise in entrapment”.

Farage claimed Orr and Jukes had merely been “contractors” who engaged in “loose pub talk, including a couple of boasts that simply were not true”. One party figure, Nadine Dorries, claimed Jukes had merely booked transport and carried bags, despite being a senior adviser integral to Reform’s operations and success for many years.

When it was put to Farage that he had thanked the bogus donors and understood what was going on, he said: “It was the middle of the byelection. I was told I had to go and meet these people. I didn’t have to, but I did. I was told they had a global family trust headquartered in London. I asked the question: is this all above board?”

blocks.caption: Nigel Farage’s keynote speech was repeatedly interrupted by protesters on Friday. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA

blocks.text: The Reform leader also insisted that the party’s internal processes would have stopped any impermissible donors and said neither Jukes nor Orr should have been carrying out fundraising. He said a suggestion by Jukes in the footage that other foreign donations had been channelled through UK intermediaries was not true and the donors did not exist.

The pair were caught out after being filmed by undercover reporters from the group Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, and broadcast by Channel 4 News on the eve of Reform’s party conference.

In the footage, Orr and Jukes appeared to help orchestrate an impermissible donation of £30,000 from the fake US donor which was used to pay for polling that would benefit Reform and made front pages of national newspapers. The money from an American company was transferred to the polling company JL Partners after being organised at the behest of Reform to boost its policies and political narrative. It was not declared to the Electoral Commission.

Jukes went on to discuss whether the US businessman could give £500,000 through a UK intermediary, who was an undercover reporter, and introduced the would-be donors to Farage at a lunch in Clacton over oysters and champagne.
The row comprehensively overshadowed the first full day of the party’s conference with every Reform politician repeatedly questioned over the scandal.

It also exposed splits at the top of the party, with Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, strongly distancing himself from Jukes and Orr. He told reporters “anyone who supports Reform is disappointed”, and added of the investigation: “It’s just not something I am personally involved in.”

He also launched a personal video about his backstory, leading to speculation he could attempt to run for the leadership as a rival to Robert Jenrick or Richard Tice if Farage were to be forced out over his financial scandals.

However, some Reform insiders are convinced Farage will part company with Yusuf before long, partly over his ambition and combative style on social media, including one post on X that saw him accused of racism towards a Somalia-born Labour councillor. Farage is understood to have used a rude term about Yusuf recently in relation to his troublemaking on social media.

One senior Reform figure said they believed Yusuf would have to go as a precondition for some sort of reconciliation with Rupert Lowe, whose party Restore Britain has eaten into the party’s voters on the hard right. Farage has recently condemned Lowe as vindictive but some of their friends believe a rapprochement could be possible if Yusuf were no longer in the party.

Reform had wanted the main event to be Farage announcing a deal with the hard-right French National Rally president, Jordan Bardella, to return small boats crossing the Channel if both parties achieve power. However, a press conference was dominated by questions about the foreign donations scandal.

blocks.caption: National Rally ​party chief, Jordan Bardella, attends a joint press conference with Farage on Friday. Photograph: Isabel Infantes/Reuters

blocks.text: Farage’s main speech was later delayed by security concerns after climate protesters disrupted Tice’s stage appearance – and more activists later repeatedly interrupted his address. While waiting to go on stage, the Reform leader danced and sung with the crowd.
He began his speech by calling for Andy Burnham to hold a general election and accusing Labour of planning to put up taxes.
Jukes issued a statement: “This was entrapment over a prolonged period of time by individuals using selective editing who had their own agenda to discredit Reform UK.”
Orr said: “I have agreed to step down from my current role at Reform UK pending the outcome of the party’s internal investigation into the conduct of the program, with which I will cooperate fully.”

The speech was light on policy but Farage at one point hinted he could look at the way judges are appointed in future – suggesting the party could look at a system of political appointments as is the case in the US.
