articles.title: Iranian town mourns after deadly strike on wedding
articles.summary:
Mourning turns to anger as residents of Kuhestak say Baloch communities are being placed in path of conflict

People in Kuhestak, a predominantly Baloch city in Iran’s southern Hormozgan…

blocks.text: People in Kuhestak, a predominantly Baloch city in Iran’s southern Hormozgan province, are mourning after a strike on a wedding killed at least four people, including a child, and injured more than 60, according to local authorities.
The blast hit at around 9.30pm on 1 September, turning a night of celebration into one of devastation for the small coastal community, which is on the strait of Hormuz.
In the aftermath, videos shared on social media by friends and relatives of the wedding couple showed rubble, flower garlands and decorations scattered among debris and bloodied shoes.

Asked about the strike on Thursday, the US vice-president, JD Vance, said the US would never target civilians in combat but that “sometimes things happen”, adding that he was sceptical of Iran’s reports. He did not acknowledge that the killings had been confirmed by an internationally recognised humanitarian body.
According to Iranian state media and people interviewed by the Guardian, the house belonged to Ali Mallahi, a local fisher who was celebrating his daughter’s wedding.
In a video published by state media, Mallahi stood amid the rubble of what had been his home and said he was saddened by the attack but thanked God that the casualties weren’t higher.
Residents said the celebrations had only just begun. Friends and family were waiting for the bride and groom, and many guests had yet to arrive for the henna ceremony.

blocks.caption: A woman weeps during a mass funeral in Kuhestak. Photograph: Razieh Poudat/AP

blocks.text: Witnesses who spoke to the Guardian said the attack had left residents angry and in deep mourning.
Ahmad*, a local barber who witnessed the aftermath, said the entire neighbourhood had been devastated by what happened.

“I don’t really have words. Ours is a small town and we all know each other and are brothers. We are all mourning. I visited the house and the media won’t report it, but it wasn’t just one house. Many houses around the site have been damaged and neighbours were directly hit by sharp objects when the explosions happened”.
“We are not carrying coffins on our shoulders, we are carrying the dark future that awaits us all in the south,” Ahmad added.
Moein Arjomand, director of the Balochistan Human Rights Documentation Network, said local responders were facing growing obstacles investigating the explosion.

“Our team has been facing a lot of difficulties due to the internet [shutdown] and witnesses and relatives telling us they were banned from speaking to any foreign rights groups and foreign media,” he said. “I tried arranging interviews for international media with the relatives, but they are worried about the consequences and I couldn’t arrange them.”
Despite the internet restrictions and apparent warnings against speaking out, locals and relatives of the couple have continued sharing videos documenting the aftermath on social media.
In one video, Yaqoob Mallahi, a relative of the bride, shared footage of his seven-year-old son, Sepehr, lying in a hospital bed with his head bandaged.

blocks.caption: Damaged buildings after the strike on a wedding party. Asked whether the US was responsible, JD Vance, the US vice-president, said ‘sometimes things happen’. Photograph: Getty Images

blocks.text: Arjomand said at least six victims remained in serious condition in the intensive care unit of a hospital in Minab, about 18 miles (30km) away.
“Bandar-e-Kuhestak is a small town and the local clinic is not equipped to handle casualties like this, so the injured were taken to the hospital in Minab,” Arjomand said.
A video posted by local activists showed the family of Amir Mohammad Karimi, the four-year-old victim, mourning over his body as he was buried on Thursday.
A 16-year-old boy, Mohammad Mallahi, was also killed by shrapnel while riding his motorbike nearby. Videos of his funeral, attended by dozens of local people, were shared online.

“We have another funeral on Friday, this time a young woman, and we will all be there,” Ahmad said. “I can only pray to Allah that no more of our blood is shed and our injured come back home from the hospital.”
Ahmad was referring to Asiyeh Molainejad, 22, another relative of the bride who was declared dead on Thursday.
Beyond the immediate grief, the attack deepened a sense among some Baloch residents and activists that civilian deaths in their communities receive comparatively little attention.

blocks.caption: Men hold red roses as they attend a mass funeral  in Kuhestak. Photograph: Razieh Poudat/AP

blocks.text: Farzin Kadkhodaei, a human rights activist from Balochistan, said the circumstances of the deaths had made the loss particularly painful.

“The human cost is devastating. These were Baloch civilians gathered for a wedding, and losing their lives in the middle of what should have been a joyful occasion is heartbreaking,” he said. “Their families are now left with unimaginable grief, while the injured have to live with the physical and emotional consequences.”

Chakar Baloch, 35, a fisher, said the attack reinforced a feeling among local people that civilians living along the Makran coast were being placed in the path of conflicts over which they had little control. “My overall view is that we are the victims. We are the people who live along the Makran coast and for years we’ve gone out to sea, struggled to earn our bread, and just wanted to stay alive,” he said.

When asked if local people were demanding answers about the strike, a Baloch resident of Sirik said western media did not understand their plight. “Who do you want me to demand answers from?” she said. “From the US that has attacked us in this war? Or the regime which has brought this war to our doorsteps? Tell me from whom I can demand and I will answer your questions.”

articles.title: Why the North Korean women's football team is so good
articles.summary: North Korea's young footballers enter the U-20 World Cup in Poland as defending champions – the 2024 title was their third. Why is the isolated state so good at the game?

image.caption: North Korea enter the tournament as defending U-20 World Cup champions, proof that their government's strategic approach to developing youth football is workingImage: Julian Medina/Sports Press Photo/IMAGO/

blocks.text: A year ago, North Korea's women successfully defended their U-17 World Cup title after defeating the Netherlands 3-0 in Morocco. It was the fourth time that the country has won the competition.

Now the country's U-20 team enter the World Cup in Poland as defending champions, having won their third World Cup in 2024. North Korea's women have clearly cemented their status as the dominant force in women's youth football.
But what is it that makes a state that, according to the United Nations, "does not have any parallel in the contemporary world" so good at youth football?

"International sport is one of the few ways to demonstrate their sovereignty, existence and identity to the international community, so this type of big success, from their point of view, is an important occasion where they can wave their national flag in front of the international audience," Dr Jung Woo Lee, a senior lecturer in Sport and Leisure Policy at the University of Edinburgh, told DW.
"At the same time, domestically, North Korea often uses sport as their propaganda tool to glorify their leaders and also how great their country is."
A clear and conscious strategy

Football is popular in the country, but recognizing that the gap to the top in senior football is much harder to close than in youth football, North Korea's leaders turned to women's youth football, where the gap is more manageable. It's also why success at this level hasn't benefited the senior team over the years. This strategy is not about pathways. It's about winning.

"The gap between established and developing clubs is also high because in many European countries, there is a professional league, and they get more support from a number of different stakeholders," Lee said.

"In youth football, I think European sport organizations highlight more on having fun when playing football. Whereas in North Korea, even if you are 13 or 14 years old, they join very highly disciplined, highly systematic and highly professionalized training regimes, so in early ages they can excel."

In Morocco, North Korea's U-17 team only conceded three goals in the entire tournament, and scored three or more on four occasions. This was a continuation of their form the year before, while the U-20 women in 2024 not only beat Argentina 6-2 but also secured three straight 1-0 victories from the quarterfinals onwards to win the tournament.

With the help of the Pyongyang International Football School where young girls are selected, developed and educated following a highly disciplined and scientific approach, North Korea has seen an opportunity and taken it.

blocks.caption: In 2025 North Korea's U-17 team won a second consecutive World Cup, making them one of the most dominant forces in youth footballImage: IPA Sport/ABACA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Regime positioning, life-changing rewards
In the eyes of North Korea, this is also a victory for the communist regime.

"You need to remember that North Korea still maintains a very strong socialist and communist regime," Lee explained. "Particularly under Kim Jong Un, they try to compare capitalist and communist regimes and show the communist regime as superior to the capitalist. Also, when I look at some of the news reports about the North Korean performance in North Korean media, they highlighted that because they are (under) the communist regime, they do whatever they can, even if they're physically exhausted.

"Then they directly compare those mentalities with capitalist countries. In capitalism, when athletes are physically exhausted and injured, there is no way to perform. They need to be changed by their coach. But in socialist systems their will is more important than (a) professional opinion from the coach or any medical staff. So North Korea frames that as a superior system."
That psychological element has seemingly given the team an edge, but beyond a strong sense of patriotism and years of disciplined work lies the motivation of a life-changing reward.

"Although we often see North Korea as quite underdeveloped and very much agricultural and people experiencing hardship, those living in Pyongyang are quite different. They are kind of special," Lee explained.

blocks.caption: Choe II-son (in red) was the breakout star of the 2024 tournament, but is unlikely to play on a bigger stageImage: Jose Pino/Sports Press Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: As an incentive, he said, the regime can give players living outside the capital residence certificates, which are required to enter Pyongyang. At the same time, many players have been given apartments.
This motivation is not to be underestimated. Life in rural North Korea is tough, with shortages in food and health care reportedly common. Living in the big city is quite different.
"This is a way to change their life. It's kind of winning a lottery in a way," Lee explained.
What next for talented generation?

For star players such as Yu Jong-hyang, topscorer at the 2025 U-17 World Cup, or Choe Il-son, a key player in both U-17 and U-20 World Cup victories in 2024, the instinctive reaction is to wonder which WSL(English top division) or NWSL(US top division) team will be trying to sign her, but that would be to forget the context in which she both lives and plays.
"I don't think it's impossible, but not so easy," Lee said of the idea of either stars playing abroad.

"First of all, (there are) the economic sanctions now imposed on North Korea," he said. "And also, whenever North Korean players joined a European league — there were a few occasions in basketball where any salary was not sent to the individual account of the players or the agent, but it goes to North Korea's government account, so I think that's another complexity involved."
While much about this team, like the country, remains a mystery, there is no denying that success at the youth level has always been the plan.

This article was originally published on September 9, 2024. It was updated on November 9, 2025 to reflect North Korea's U-17 World Cup title win. It was also updated on September 4, 2026 ahead of the kickoff of the U-20 World Cup in Poland.

articles.title: Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage and Russia is the chief suspect
articles.summary: Germany has blamed Russia for an attack on Leipzig airport but there has been a series of suspicious incidents elsewhere.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Germany said the attack at Leipzig airport was part of a pattern of "Russian hybrid operations" in Europe
BySarah Rainsford
Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent
As summer temperatures in Europe smashed records this summer and many politicians shifted to holiday mode, Russia remained focused on its war.
Not only did its military attacks across Ukraine intensify last month, becoming ever more deadly for civilians, Russia also appears to have escalated its sabotage campaign across Europe.
This time, military and defence sector sites were the prime target.
A full month after drones packed with explosives were found at Leipzig's airport, used by Ukraine to transport military goods, Germany's interior minister has declared that "Russia is responsible".
Russia's President Vladimir Putin is demanding proof, as always, and his officials call the accusation "absurd".
But the drones were just a dramatic start. August then brought a series of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia.
Some of the affected countries have already blamed Russia; others are still investigating and some fires may eventually be ruled accidental, exactly as such attacks are designed to seem.
Poland's interior minister is clear.

"There are many, many signals that Russia is changing its strategy and intensifying its activities, including terrorist and sabotage activities," Marcin Kierwiński said, warning people to be on their guard.
August campaign across Europe
4 August Germany: The first drone at Leipzig airport is discovered.
10 August Bulgaria: A major fire breaks out at a factory of the defence firm EMCO, with initial reports that a truck ignited during a fuel delivery.
13 August Italy: A fire at KNDS Ammo Italy outside Rome triggers a large explosion.

The local prosecutor is looking into possible outside interference, La Repubblica newspaper reports. Publicly, his office will only confirm that a case has been opened for negligent disaster against "unknown persons".
15 August Estonia: The Milrem Robotics factory in Tallinn, which the Kyiv Post says supplies drones to Ukraine, goes up in flames. Two suspects are arrested.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal says the possibility of Russian sabotage is being "taking seriously" by investigators.

25 August Slovakia: Police announce they have averted an arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer and seized a "large amount of incendiary mixture". The firm itself blames Russia and police arrest three suspects who they say were "following orders". Slovakia is Russia's close ally in Europe.
30 August Poland: A country which is heavily targeted for sabotage reports two more fires.
One is in Lublin at a company which produces helicopter components. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said arson "cannot be ruled out".
An attack on the drone producer, WB Group, is clearer cut. A masked man is caught on CCTV throwing incendiary devices. Tusk calls it a "continuation of Russia's escalatory activities".
The pattern has continued into September with two Bulgarians arrested in Munich, Germany, for suspected arson after throwing incendiary devices from a car at defence firm Rhode & Schwartz.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The 31 August fire at Skarżysko-Kamienna targeted one of Poland's biggest defence firms

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
The 31 August fire at Skarżysko-Kamienna targeted one of Poland's biggest defence firms
Why is this happening now?
Attacks on military and defence targets are not new, although previous acts of sabotage linked to Russia include more puzzling targets - such as an Ikea store and a Polish paint store.
The novelty now is the concentration of cases.
"The intensity of military sites being attacked we've seen over the past couple of weeks is unusual," Daniela Richterova of the Department of War Studies at King's College says.
She links the spike to developments in Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
"We've basically seen Ukraine take the war to Russia and strike deep inside Russian territory…They [Moscow] are under pressure, they have to do something."
Whilst some sabotage is staged to sow chaos or fear, Richterova believes the Kremlin's aim right now is "coercive signalling": pressuring countries to stop supporting Kyiv by raising the stakes.
After a slow start, Germany is Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid.
There are other theories.
To some, Russia is less concerned about "turning off the taps" of supplies to Ukraine and more about testing Nato for weaknesses.

"Russia is probing the boundaries of what's acceptable and collecting information on the results. They find out what works, and what's vulnerable," argues Keir Giles from the Chatham House think tank.
He sees the sabotage campaign as preparation for the "next phase", as he puts it, of Russia's aggression in Europe.
"They're assessing the willingness of the victim country to actually do something about it."

The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), which tracks sabotage cases, points to a previous surge in 2024 when Ukraine's allies began allowing it to use Western-supplied weapons deeper inside Russia.
2024 was the year of the parcel bomb plot, when Russia was accused of sending packages containing liquid explosive to the UK and Poland.
One ignited shortly before it was loaded on to a DHL cargo plane. It is thought this was a test run for something significantly bigger.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Four parcels were sent from Lithuania to the UK and Poland in 2024 - two caught fire, at a warehouse in the UK and at Leipzig's airport

blocks.text: Image source, Police handout
Four parcels were sent from Lithuania to the UK and Poland in 2024 - two caught fire, at a warehouse in the UK and at Leipzig's airport
"That was a marked high in terms of their willingness to inflict mass casualties," Giles adds.
It was a step so serious, the White House contacted the Kremlin to tell it to stop. Russia had probed and found the limit.
But the attacks have continued. German media on Friday quoted a federal police report that lists more than 165 suspected sabotage cases nationwide this year, though they don't say who is responsible.
Who are the suspected saboteurs?
Reports from Germany suggest the men who loaded and launched the drones at Leipzig's airport were Russian, and at least one may have entered the country specially for this job.
That would be unusual.
The vast majority of sabotage attacks in Europe have been carried out by Russian proxies: its so-called "gig economy saboteurs".
They are usually Russian-speakers from former Soviet states, recruited online and driven by the cash, not political conviction.
In one case the BBC reported from Poland, the saboteurs-for-hire had previously fought for Ukraine as volunteers.
The "handlers" are generally thought to remain in Russia, co-ordinating operations online.
The IISS likened the proxies they used to kamikaze drones: cheap and easy to launch in large numbers, but disposable.
The amateurs can be sloppy or reckless, though. In the parcel plot, one man failed to find a pick-up point and the whole mission had to be aborted.
So if Moscow did send professionals for the Leipzig drone launch, it suggests it wanted precision - and success.
In fact, the devices appear to have malfunctioned.
Nato faced with Soviet-style campaign

Russia's sabotage operations seem to come from the Cold War playbook. Daniela Richterova's research shows very similar targets on Soviet sabotage lists, and agents-saboteurs were used in much the same way.
The idea, she says, was to have small, deniable attacks in peace-time that would escalate in times of war.
"I think we are still in the grey zone between the two, but the kind of attacks we've seen in the past weeks shrink that zone," she says. "And I think that increases the risk of what happens next."
As Nato scrambles to respond, questions like how many small, individual attacks add up to a sustained Russian assault - and demand action - remain unanswered.
Perhaps riskier than all is the potential for escalation by accident.
What if the exploding parcel had gone off mid-air and caused a crash? What if the Leipzig drone had brought down a plane?
"I think it could result in a big attack," Richterova says. "Then Nato, in this heightened security environment, would not be able to ignore that, and have to react."

articles.title: After renewed US-Iran strikes - how could the conflict end?
articles.summary: Three experts give their BBC their thoughts on whether an imminent end to the conflict is likely.

blocks.text: Jason Campbell, Senior Fellow at the Middle East Institute, Washington DC

The problem is we still do not know definitively what the US strategic objectives are in Iran. The White House is persistently re-evaluating what it is willing to live with from a political standpoint.
It was assumed the military component would be enough for a quick victory and that has not had the desired effect.
What we are seeing is different levers - both military and economic - that the US is trying to pull at.

Right now, the administration appears satisfied with some form of statis. I think they are satisfied with maintaining the blockade and with allowing some periodic targeting against Iran's capability to upset the shipping lane in the strait.
US officials are hopeful that the new sanctions will be enough to compel the Iranian regime to come to the negotiating table in a weaker position.

US forces have seemingly been able to facilitate a sufficient trickle through the Strait of Hormuz in recent days to avert an oil-price shock or a global economic collapse. But those were not the US objectives when starting the war.
My sense is that Iran is likely to demand a high price to get to a resolution, which is likely to remain politically untenable for the Trump administration.
Dr Aniseh Bassiri Tabrizi, Associate Fellow with Chatham House's Middle East and North Africa Programme, London

I do not think the latest strikes really alter Iranian calculations on the war. I think Tehran is preparing for an increased squeeze on its economy, and a continuation of the on and off attacks which we have seen over the past couple of months. Their intent will be to respond to these attacks in a proportionate manner in order not to spiral a larger conflict.

On the economic side, obviously this is likely to hurt the Iranian economy which has already been affected by the war and has had underlying structural issues anyway, as we know from the December and January demonstrations in Iran.
But I do not feel like there is the sense from the Iranian side that the economic squeeze is going to alter the Iranian calculation any time soon, including on any negotiations.

That does not mean Iran is not looking for an off ramp, but I think what we are seeing is that it is waiting for the US to go back to the MoU, or to at least offer some sort of concession. Tehran does not want to cave in to US pressure or alter its own approach in response to sanctions or additional attacks.
Nicholas Hopton, Distinguished Fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute think tank in London and former UK ambassador to Iran

The latest spike in military action is not going to produce Iran's capitulation - it is just the latest twist. Economic pressure is also unlikely to work because China, Russia and many other countries which trade with Iran are not going to support unilateral US sanctions.
Iran can continue to disrupt the Strait of Hormuz - they have a thumb on the jugular of the global economy.
What is the White House's exit strategy?
Well, the US has already found it. If Trump was able to put a sustained effort into negotiating the deal outlined in June's MoU, that is the off-ramp.
Not only would a deal give the US a kind of victory because it would weaken the hardliners in the Islamic Republic, but also reassure everyone that Iran is not going to get a nuclear weapon.
There is a silver bullet in the MoU which is the lifting of all US sanctions on Iran.

What lifting those sanctions would do over time is weaken Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp (IRGC). Economic engagement between the outside world and Iran in a new way would gradually force radical political and social change - so you end up with an Islamic regime, but of a very different nature.

Of course, that would not be straightforward to achieve, because of extensive IRGC penetration of the Iranian economy. But it should work, if given enough time and if the US and its partners exercised strategic patience which, sadly, is in short supply at this point.
For the time being, I think we're going to carry on with a messy, inconclusive situation that is bad for everyone.

articles.title: UK ministers hit back at Argentinian Falklands claim and insist islands remain British
articles.summary: Defence secretary says ‘winds of change’ remarks by Argentina’s president are more about domestic politics

blocks.text: British ministers have hit back after the Argentinian president said “winds of change” favourable to his country’s claim to the Falklands were “blowing around the world”.

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said the UK would “resolutely uphold” the self-determination of the islands after the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, said his country needed to take them back.
Miliband said in a post on X: “The UK’s position on the Falkland Islands is unwavering.
“The islands are British and will remain so because that is the overwhelming position of the Islanders.
“Their right of self-determination is paramount, grounded in international law and we will resolutely uphold it.”
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said Milei’s statement by “tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands”.
He added on X: “The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British. Our commitment to the Falklands is absolute and unshakeable.”
Lucy Powell, the education secretary, also insisted the islands were British, adding: “We will defend the right of those who live in the Falkland Islands to determine their own future.”
The latest diplomatic spat over the South Atlantic archipelago came after comments by the US president, Donald Trump, who has cast doubt on American support for British control of the islands.

blocks.caption: Mount Tumbledown behind Stanley on the Falkland Islands, which Argentina calls Malvinas. Photograph: Ricardo Mazalán/AP

blocks.text: The US has traditionally remained neutral on the Falklands’ sovereignty, while recognising Britain’s de facto control over them.
Britain and Argentina fought a war over the islands in 1982, when British forces defeated Argentinian troops, who had landed there to stake a territorial claim.
In more recent years, the British oil company Rockhopper and the Israeli company Navitas have been developing the Sea Lion oil field, 140 miles to the north of the islands.
Asked on Monday whether he could review British sovereignty over the islands as a way to push the UK to spend more on defence, Trump said: “I always review every position. That’s just one of many.”

And on Thursday, when quizzed about whether the US would back the UK in the event of an Argentinian invasion, he referred to the government’s refusal to let him use British bases in his initial attack on Iran earlier this year.
“Don’t forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me,” he told GB News. “Your country was not there to help me.”

He added: “The Falklands is very interesting because your country is not the same country it was 20 years ago, 25 years ago. That was a long time [ago], you went there and you just took it back very quickly. There was no games, so I don’t know if you’re prepared to do that.”

In his statement on Thursday night, Milei highlighted Trump’s comments, saying: “President Trump declared that the US is re-evaluating its historic position in relation to the Malvinas [the Argentinian name for the Falklands].”

He added: “The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come.”
He also said companies developing oil “behind the back of the Argentine government” would be barred from doing business in Argentina.
Rockhopper’s shares dropped 7% in early trading on Friday.

articles.title: 'Layer upon layer of miracles': How Nepal flood survivors were rescued from tunnel
articles.summary: From searching for a buried tunnel entrance to blowing up rocks the size of cars, rescuers had to surmount multiple challenges to reach survivors.

blocks.text: A tunnelling expert involved in the rescue operation at a blocked Nepalese hydropower tunnel has described to the BBC how they managed to reach survivors.

Arnold Dix has been advising Nepal's hydropower authorities on how to dig through the blocked tunnel to Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, which was one of several stations hit by last week's massive flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border.
"It's like layer upon layer of layer of miracles" that they found two men on Friday, he said, given that the multiple challenges they faced.
The first hurdle was to locate the hydropower station, in a landscape rendered nearly unrecognisable by the flood that has so far killed 1,300 people.

"I've never known an rescue operation where you had to look for an entrance of a tunnel that was previously up the hill, that was now underground. You can imagine the enormity of the avalanche, it completely buried the entrance," said Dix, who is the president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association.

Using engineering techniques, old topographic maps, satellite imagery of the area after the disaster, video footage from helicopters, and "anything else we could find on the surface of the mountain such as power poles", Dix and his team triangulated the likely position of the entrance and started digging.
They found it - but the next challenge was to locate the survivors.
"We knew they would be up ahead, but we didn't know where exactly. So you just have to start digging in the right direction. And you listen out if you can hear anybody," he said.
Rescuers had to get through a tunnel blocked entirely by mud and rocks - some bigger than cars - and had to resort to using explosives to clear the way.
"We had to use explosives which we normally never do because of the risk of blowing up people [trapped in the tunnel] and blowing ourselves up," said Dix.
He credited the Nepalese army for doing "a wonderful job" in managing the explosions with precision to ensure they would not destabilise the tunnel.
At the same time, they discovered the tunnel was still full of water.
Using excavators and pumping machines, Nepalese rescuers dug a series of trenches from the tunnel all the way to the river outside, so they could drain the water.
Finally, they had to dig a passageway, "a tiny tunnel the size of a person", through the debris at the top of the tunnel.
The advantage of this location "is that you can use the original tunnel's roof as your little tunnel's roof. Also, it mitigates risk of flooding," said Dix.
In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices.
According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay".
Shortly after that, they pulled out Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan, alive.
But with dozens of people still thought to be trapped inside the tunnel, the work is far from over.
Dix estimated that they had dug about 60m from the entrance by now, and they would need to dig another 150m more to reach the hydropower station located deep inside the mountain.

Rescuers are hoping that the debris from the flood would not have reached the station, because if it did, "there would be all kinds of complications - anybody in the station could have been hit by rocks and mud or it could be flooded".
The team on the ground are still facing significant dangers.

"Up ahead, even now, we might run into water which would drown the people tunnelling," said Dix. "And we also have the risk of another flood outside happening, so water could come from behind. So there's the risk of facing water on both ends."
But, buoyed by Friday's successful rescue, the team is now hopeful it will reach more survivors in time.
"It's a big relief, that we are on the right track. And it gives us renewed energy that our thinking [on how to conduct the rescue] works... we have never done something like this before."
Dix said they are now heading towards what he called the "Goldilocks zone" which would be "more friendly to life".
This zone is at the uppermost level of the hydropower station where there is some space where survivors may be located.
"We got two people out. If we were playing at a casino, some might say it's time to walk away, but we say game on, time to take on the house."

articles.title: 2026 Beethoven Festival evokes a sense of home
articles.summary: The motto of this year's festival in Bonn is "Home/At Home," featuring musicians from diverse cultures presenting pieces from their homelands.

image.caption: After 10 years, the Beethovenfest in Bonn returns to its old home, the BeethovenhalleImage: Marc John/Bonn.digital/picture alliance

blocks.text: Four trumpeters will be scattered throughout the concert hall, accompanied by organ music, promising a magnificent auditory experience in Bonn's newly renovated Beethovenhalle.

The piece "A Call to the Heavens" was composed by Stefan Behrisch specifically for the opening of this year's Beethovenfest. Additionally, the London Symphony Orchestra, led by principal conductor Sir Antonio Pappano, will perform Ludwig van Beethoven's "Die Weihe des Hauses" ("The Consecration of the House") as well as Bruckner's Symphony No. 9 at the opening concert on September 4.

blocks.caption: The Beethovenhalle aims to make everyone feel at home Image: Marc John/Bonn.digital/picture alliance

blocks.text: For nine years, Bonn's Beethovenhalle, a designated historic landmark, was unavailable for the festival. But now, as Philipp Seliger, spokesperson for the Beethoven Festival explains, "we have a large concert hall again with its excellent original acoustics." He adds: "We can once again invite major renowned orchestras because we have the appropriate stage and infrastructure." This also prompted Hungarian star pianist, András Schiff, to perform at the festival this year.
A musical home for everyone

blocks.caption: Juri de Marco founded a community choir in Bonn's Tannenbusch neighborhoodImage: Beethovenfest Bonn

blocks.text: The new hall is not only intended to make stars and major orchestras feel at home — the audience and local musicians ought to feel that way too. Indeed, for local musicians, there is a specially designed "Festival Salon" where local communities and bands can create their own programs. And anyone can come by and participate in the "Meet your band" project, which is an accessible, free program for people who otherwise wouldn't visit a classical concert hall.

The Beethovenfest also reaches out to people in neighborhoods across the city, right where they live. For over a year, as a part of this effort, Juri de Marco and the "Community Choir" have been encouraging people to sing and improvise, regardless of whether they can read music.

blocks.caption: Steven Walter addresses the topic of home not only in his music, but also in lectures and in discussion forumsImage: Bjorn Kietzmann/DW

blocks.text: "For me, home is more a feeling than it is a place. It's where you can rely on a genuine social network, where people notice when you are absent," says festival director Steven Walter. who has lived in various places around the world himself. "Everywhere I go, my sense of well-being depends on my social connections."
Beethoven reinterpreted

Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1850, and died in Vienna in 1827. Next year marks the 200th anniversary of his death, and to celebrate it, pianist Kit Armstrong with conductor Jan Caeyers, along with his orchestra "Le Concert Olympique," are launching "Beethoven 27," a major Beethoven cycle. In nine concerts, they will present entirely new interpretations of Beethoven's nine symphonies, as well as his sonatas and piano concertos.

blocks.caption: 'Beethoven 27' is the name of the project in which Kit Armstrong plays the pianoImage: SALVATORE DI NOLFI/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

blocks.text: The first three concerts will be presented at this year's Beethovenfest. Caeyers has devoted himself to Beethoven not only as a conductor but also as a musicologist. He is the author of the acclaimed biography "Beethoven: A life." Even so, Caeyers says he is far from finished discovering the composer.

"Every time I immerse myself in Beethoven, new and unexpected doors open. That's what keeps me fascinated," Caeyers told DW. Pianist Kit Armstrong feels the same way. "There isn't just one Beethoven," he said. "There are countless images and perspectives of Beethoven, including many that emerged long after his death. Those perspectives should also inform the way we interpret his music today."
Spotlight on Georgia

This year's Beethovenfest artists will introduce music from their homelands. Among them are Senegalese kora player Momi Maiga and Palestinian-Syrian pianist Aeham Ahmad, who gained global renown for playing the piano amid the rubble of the Syrian civil war.

blocks.caption: Violinist Lisa Batiashvili also supports young talent from her native Georgia, including composer Tsotne Zedginidze Image: picture-alliance/dpa/P. Zinken

blocks.text: Violinist Lisa Batiashvili, who was born in Georgia, is this year's artist in residence at the Beethovenfest. Performing with the Dresden Philharmonic, she will present works from her homeland as part of the program "City Lights" — a personal tribute to Georgia, which the festival is spotlighting this year.

As part of the festival's long-running "Campus" youth exchange program, young musicians from Georgia and Germany will collaborate, with Beethoven's music being performed alongside works by leading Georgian composers. The entire ensemble will also perform Heinrich Schütz's five-part motet "Verleih uns Frieden gnädiglich" ("Grant Us Gracious Peace").

Musicians from Germany's National Youth Orchestra and the Tbilisi Youth Orchestra held their joint rehearsal residency in June, developing their own artistic vision and program for Beethovenfest. The project also explores how young artists see themselves in a country facing political turmoil, where the path toward Europe has repeatedly shifted course.

blocks.caption: During rehearsals in Tbilisi, conductor Mirian Khukhunaishvili (left) and composer Tsotne Zedginidze (right) discuss his new workImage: Beethovenfest

blocks.text: 17-year-old composer and pianist Tsotne Zedginidze is regarded as one of Georgia's most extraordinary young musical talents. He was commissioned to write the Campus project's new work.
Beyond classical music

Crossovers, musical fusion and new ideas for the future of music remain central to this year's Beethovenfest. Two musical worlds will come together with kora player Momi Maiga joining the string orchestra "Ensemble Resonanz" to improvise on Beethoven's music.

blocks.caption: Composer and performer Brittany J. Green combines sound, video, movement and text in her workImage: Adley Haywood

blocks.text: American composer Brittany J. Green will experiment with artificial intelligence and visual effects in her work "gLitchED dreams//invisible BEINGS." Performed with the music collective "Alarm Will Sound," the piece creates a sonic landscape inspired by the digital age. "We're looking for the Beethovens of our time," says Philipp Seliger, "including people who aren't necessarily composers of classical music."
The Beethovenfest runs from Sept 3 through Oct 3, 2026. DW is a media partner and co-shareholder of the festival.
This article was originally written in German.
Deep dive into classical music

articles.title: Bond yields are soaring to multi-decade highs. What does that mean for Canadian consumers?
articles.summary: The bond market is experiencing a steep, global sell-off, creating waves for consumers and investors alike. Here's what you need to know about how the bond market can affect you.

image.caption: Traders gather on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in this 2010 file photo. The bond market is experiencing a steep, global sell-off. (Richard Drew/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Business
The bond market is experiencing a steep, global sell-off, creating waves for consumers and investors alike. Here's what you need to know about how the bond market can affect you.
Canadians can expect higher mortgage rates, stronger returns on GICs
With global bond yields surging to multi-decade highs, a previously mundane corner of the financial world is now a hot topic on Wall Street.

For the average Canadian, it means higher borrowing costs for some products, such as mortgages and auto loans, but also stronger returns on other products, such as other guaranteed investment certificates (GICs) and money market funds.

Let's start with the basics. When you buy a bond, you're effectively lending money for a predetermined amount of time to the issuer. That could be the federal government, provinces, municipalities or a private company. Investors are typically paid interest until the maturity date, when they get the face value of the bond back.

So, what's a bond yield? It's the annual return an investor earns from holding a bond, expressed as a percentage. After bonds are issued, they can be traded on the open market, causing their prices to shift. When bond prices drop, yields rise. This is because investors get the same interest payments for a lower buy-in price.

Until recently, the global bond market was pretty sleepy. That's because central bankers around the world kept interest rates at near-zero for more than a decade following the 2008 financial crisis. Now, a growing number of investors see rate hikes on the horizon as central banks look to tamp down sticky inflation.
When a central bank raises interest rates, newly issued bonds offer higher payouts, making existing lower-paying bonds less valuable.
Higher inflation puts pressure on central banks
Right now, the bond market is experiencing a steep, global sell-off. From the United States, to Germany, Japan and Canada, yields have jumped to multi-year or even multi-decade highs.

"What's going on there? Well, when you see a substantial movement, usually it's because there is more than one thing happening at once," Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said on Wednesday, after the central bank's latest interest rate decision was announced.
Inflation fears and concerns about ballooning government debt are feeding expectations for the Bank of Canada and its global peers to raise their trend-setting interest rates.
"Central banks' tolerance for higher inflation is limited," said Macklem. "That is causing the market to build in the possibility of future interest rate hikes."

According to the latest Statistics Canada data, gas prices were a key driver of higher inflation in July. On Wednesday, the Bank of Canada said global oil prices are persistently high, with no end in sight for the U.S.-led war with Iran, which has disrupted seaborne crude traffic in the region. U.S. benchmark oil prices have soared nearly 60 per cent year-to-date.

items: Inflation risks rise with higher fuel costs and new U.S. tariffs, Bank of Canada governor warns
'Measured confidence': RBC, TD Bank, CIBC share optimistic outlook for Canada's economy

blocks.text: At the same time, the bank sees the Canada-U.S. trade war pushing up costs for businesses, which could feed into consumer prices over time. Macklem noted the AI infrastructure buildout is stoking demand for new corporate bond issuance, lowering prices for previously issued bonds.
"All those things are tending to work in the same direction to boost global bond yields," Macklem said.
Inflationary impact of counter-tariffs expected to be 'relatively modest': Bank of Canada governor
Canada's 10-year government bond yield hit a two-year high on Wednesday, after the Bank of Canada signalled inflation risks are rising.

Because Canadian banks can invest risk-free with the government, government bond yields set the floor for all other lending. Fixed-rate mortgages, auto loans and other forms of credit are linked to five-year and 10-year government bonds, meaning the higher the yields for those bonds are, the higher the banks set their interest rates for those loans.
For those looking to invest their savings, rising bond yields force banks to raise their GIC rates to stay competitive, boosting guaranteed returns.
'A good time to lock in your mortgage'
True North Mortgage founder and CEO Dan Eisner says savvy borrowers are locking in rates.

"Fixed mortgage rates won't drop substantially until yields do. Yields aren't likely to enter a sustained downward trend unless signs of deeper economic softening gain momentum and inflation pressures ease," Eisner wrote in a blog post on Wednesday.

"It's a good time to lock in your mortgage rate if you're looking to buy a home or renew your mortgage, as fixed rate movement is likely to resemble a rollercoaster for the next while, or at least until we see some clarity on geopolitical activity and U.S. trade."

Google Trends data show Canadians are taking a keen interest in the ongoing bond market upheaval. The volume of inquiries about the bond market over the past month is up 5,000 per cent on a yearly basis, according to the search engine giant.
No 'dysfunction' in Canada's bond market
Macklem said while there has been some "spillover" from higher global yields into Canada's bond market, Canada's yield curve sits well below that of U.S. government bonds.

Speaking at Wednesday's press conference in Ottawa, Bank of Canada Senior Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers reassured investors that Canada's bond market, while affected by global trends, is not necessarily in dangerous territory.
"I think it's important to distinguish between volatility and dysfunction or instability when prices and yields are moving, because investors are repricing risk," she told reporters.

"The vulnerability that we have talked about in our previous financial stability reports really comes when you get leveraged investors unwinding their positions quickly, and liquidity starts to dry up," she added, referring to investors such as hedge funds and non-bank asset managers who use borrowed money to fund their investment strategies.
"That's the risk we worry about. We don't see that happening right now."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. He was also a Columbia University energy journalism fellow for 2025.

articles.title: South Korea pushes back on reports it is readying Hormuz deployment amid US pressure
articles.summary:
Seoul reportedly seeking parliamentary approval to send military assets to Middle East but president’s office plays down claims

South Korea is reviewing a possible deployment of military…

blocks.text: South Korea is reviewing a possible deployment of military assets to the strait of Hormuz amid pressure from Donald Trump over Seoul’s reluctance to provide support in the region, according to domestic media reports.

Citing unnamed government and military sources, the reportspublished on Thursday and Friday said preparations were under way and that the government intended to seek parliamentary approval for a new deployment. The reports, which appeared in major South Korean outlets, said the exact scale and timing have not been agreed.

But the presidential office pushed back, telling the Guardian that such reports were “different from the facts” and that “nothing related to the matter has been decided”, though it said the review was “continuing”.

An official said: “Our government has been closely discussing with the international community ways to make practical contributions for the speedy restoration of free navigation in the strait of Hormuz and peace and stability in the Middle East.”

According to reports, the assets under consideration include a P-8 Poseidon aircraft, which would mark South Korea’s first overseas deployment of a maritime patrol aircraft, and a naval logistics support ship to provide rear support.
One outlet, Seoul Broadcasting System, additionally reported that an explosive ordnance disposal team from the navy’s underwater demolition unit was part of the package.
Any new deployment in principle would require review by the national security council, a cabinet resolution and approval from the national assembly.
South Korea is highly dependent on the strait of Hormuz, importing more than 90% of its primary energy, including roughly 70% of crude oil through the waterway.

blocks.caption: The office of South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, said ‘nothing related to the matter has been decided’ in response to the media reports. Photograph: YONHAP/EPA

blocks.text: In 2020, the government of the then president Moon Jae-in expanded the mandate of an existing anti-piracy unit off the coast of Somalia to cover the strait of Hormuz, rather than seeking parliamentary approval for a new deployment.

South Korea’s defence minister, Ahn Gyu-back, in March told parliament that any deployment to the strait would require the national assembly’s consent given how different the mission would be from the unit’s existing anti-piracy mandate.

The reports come amid growing strains in the US-South Korea alliance. Trump has repeatedly complained in public that Seoul turned down his request for help over Iran, claiming in August that South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had told him “No, thanks” despite the US stationing tens of thousands of troops on the peninsula.
Days later, he ordered the Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercises to be scaled back, shortening the drills by six days.

Relations between the two allies have also been strained by delays implementing a $350bn investment package Seoul agreed with Washington last year, reports that the US had restricted intelligence sharing with South Korea, and by a dispute over a data breach at the South Korean e-commerce company Coupang.
Separately, Seoul has expressed interest in taking part in any renewed US-North Korea diplomacy, as Trump signals openness to another meeting with Kim Jong-un.

articles.title: Labour asks Met police to launch criminal inquiry into Reform UK donations after undercover report – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Two key aides to Nigel Farage have stepped down pending an internal investigation

Lee Anderson, the Reform UK chief whip and party chair, has said that James Orr and Dan…

blocks.text: Two aides suspended over donations allegations have 'no chance of coming back', says Reform UK's chair Lee Anderson

Lee Anderson, the Reform UK chief whip and party chair, has said that James Orr and Dan Jukes – the two aides primarily involved in the apparent plot exposed by an undercover investigation to evade electoral law – were suspended and won’t be coming back.
In an interview on Sky News this morning, Anderson said:
double quotation mark[Orr and Jukes] were told they had to step down. They have stepped down. And that’s got to be the right thing to do.

The presenter, Kamali Melbourne, put it to Anderson that Orr, head of policy at the party, and Jukes, a key aide to Nigel Farage, were both very important figures in the party and asked if there was any chance they could “come back”. Anderson replied:

double quotation markNo, there’s no chance of them coming back. They’ve stepped aside. We’re a serious party, you know, and sometimes in politics, you have to make tough decisions, harsh decisions. I think this probably was an easier decision, being given the option to stand down. They have gone. Like I said, they’ve left the building and our focus now is on the conference today.
Key events

items: nowAnderson says Farage won't quit over undercover report into donations, and 'country needs him'
16m agoTwo aides suspended over donations allegations have 'no chance of coming back', says Reform UK's chair Lee Anderson
28m agoFarage personally has 'serious questions to answer' over alleged Reform UK plot to evade electoral law, Ed Davey says
39m agoLabour asks Met police to launch criminal inquiry into Reform UK donations, as two party aides involved step down

blocks.text: Anderson says Farage won't quit over undercover report into donations, and 'country needs him'

In a separate interview, on Times Radio, Lee Anderson, the Reform UK chief whip and party chair, insisted there was no chance of Nigel Farage resigning over the undercover investigation into party donations.
Anderson said:

double quotation markI don’t think Nigel has got any questions on this. The two people involved, they have gone. They have left the building. I keep saying this time and time again. They have gone. That is the right thing to do. They are not coming back and Nigel is going nowhere … Nigel is an honest man. I have known him for many years now. The party has done the right thing by launching this investigation. Nigel will be on the main stage later on explaining our first 100 days in government. He is not going anywhere. The country needs him.

While James Orr and Dan Jukes are the main focus of the investigation, the film shown by Channel 4 News suggests Farage himself also had some knowledge of the proposal for a US-based supporter to donate £500,000 to the party by channelling it through his UK-based son. Foreigners are not allowed to donate to UK political parties, and donating via proxies in this manner is also banned.
Farage is filmed attending an oyster bar lunch where he thought he was meeting the father and son. But the ‘son’ was an undercover reporter, and the ‘father’ an actor hired to play the part.
After discussion of how the money from the UK might be given to the party via the son, Farage is recorded telling them: “Thank you both.”
Farage personally has 'serious questions to answer' over alleged Reform UK plot to evade electoral law, Ed Davey says

Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, says Nigel Farage was ultimately responsible for the apparent attempt to evade electoral law on donations exposed by the undercover investigation shown on Channel 4 News.
In a post on social media this morning, he says:
double quotation markSo much for this being a “hoax” then. Clearly very serious questions for Farage to answer given his role in the meeting. The buck stops with him.

Davey was referring to the way Reform UK, in its first response to the undercover report last night, said it had “been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded, climate change activists posing as would-be party donors”.
Labour asks Met police to launch criminal inquiry into Reform UK donations, as two party aides involved step down

Good morning. Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, is speaking on the main day of his party’s conference in Birmingham. It has been a bad summer for the party. After having a large lead over the other parties in opinion polls for over a year, the lead collapsed after Andy Burnham became PM, and now Reform UK and Labour are basically neck and neck. Farage has been embroiled in the scandal over his failure to declare a £5m donation. And last night, on the eve of Farage’s big speech, Channel 4 News broadcast the findings of a long, undercover investigation showing leading Reform UK figures apparently plotting to evade UK law on electoral donations.
Here is Rowena Mason’s story.
You can read the Channel 4 News write-up here. But to fully appreciate how strong the evidence against Reform UK is, it is best to watch the half-hour report in full.
There are two developments this morning.

items: Reform UK says the two senior Reform officials most implicated in the apparent plot to evade electoral law are stepping down pending an investigation. In a statement released about half an hour ago, a Reform UK spokesperson said:

blocks.text: double quotation markReform UK has launched an investigation following the broadcast of a Channel 4 News programme. Both individuals involved have stepped down from their respective positions pending the outcome of the investigation. The party believes it is important that the investigation is allowed to proceed independently and without prejudice. No further comment will be made while the investigation is ongoing.
This is a reference to James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, a senior aide to Farage.

items: The Labour party has written to the Metropolitan police calling for a criminal investigation. In her letter to Mark Rowley, the Met commissioner, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, says:

blocks.text: double quotation markWe … believe there is a proper basis for a police investigation into whether offences under PPERA [Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000] have been committed, including, but not necessarily limited to: (a) offences under section 61(1) concerning evasion of restrictions on donations; (b) any offence arising from knowingly providing false information to, or withholding material information from, the registered treasurer in circumstances falling within section 61(2); (c) any offence arising from Reform UK’s acceptance or retention of impermissible donations, including the £32,500 of polling expenditure, if the evidential and reporting facts establish the necessary elements; and (d) any related offence concerning the accuracy or completeness of statutory donation returns. We understand that political finance matters also fall within the regulatory remit of the Electoral Commission. We are not suggesting that a police investigation should displace the commission’s role; rather, given the apparent possibility of criminal conduct, we believe the allegations should be brought formally to the attention of the police so that the appropriate authorities can determine the proper investigative route.
Here is the agenda for the day.

11.05am: The main day of Reform UK’s conference opens with tributes to Ann Widdecombe. After that the main speakers on the stage are chief whip Lee Anderson at 11.30am; Welsh leader Dan Thomas at 11.45am; home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf at noon; Jordon Bardella, president of the French National Rally party at 12.30pm: Matt Goodwin at 3pm; Sarah Pochin MP at 3.15pm; deputy leader Richard Tice at 3.30pm: and Nigel Farage at 3.50pm. There are also fringe meetings through the day.
1pm: Farage and Bardella hold a press conference.
Afternoon: Kemi Badenoch is on a visit in West Sussex.

articles.title: How Volkswagen's huge workforce became a costly burden
articles.summary: The struggling German carmaker plans to cut up to 100,000 jobs from its 630,000-strong workforce. How did VW's headcount get so bloated, and will the cuts be enough to survive the Chinese EV…

image.caption: VW has 60% more employees than Toyota, which makes a similar number of carsImage: Moritz Frankenberg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Volkswagen has built one of the largest workforces in the global auto industry.
At nearly 630,000 people — 680,000 if you count joint ventures in China — VW employs around 60% more workers than Toyota, 140% more than Stellantis and nearly 240% more than Ford.

That headcount was once a sign of Germany's industrial might and VW's huge profits. Now, it's become a massive burden, one that's forcing the company to make painful job cuts to survive against agile Chinese competitors.

After already trimming thousands of positions last year as profits came under pressure, Volkswagen is now preparing to slash 50,000 additional jobs worldwide, including tens of thousands in Germany. The proposal got the backing of the VW Supervisory Board on Thursday, September 2.
VW also wants to close four German factories, a plan that the supervisory board on Thursday stopped short of agreeing to implement right away.

These cuts include VW luxury brands like Porsche and Audi. Other German automakers and suppliers are facing similar pressures. Mercedes-Benz is planning to cut several thousand jobs, and suppliers like Bosch have announced large cost savings.
How VW got to this point
Much of VW's headcount issue stems from long-standing strategic decisions.

Meghan Ostertag, an analyst for economic policy at the US-based Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, says VW's much larger workforce was needed because the firm chose to control more stages of production than its peers.

"The company makes many of its components and software internally, increasing the demand for labor and, of course, labor costs," Ostertag told DW, adding that factory expenses in Germany can be "up to twice those of the competition."
Other experts point to an aggressive acquisition strategy over the years, which brought brands including Skoda, Porsche, SEAT and Bugatti into the VW fold — not to mention several truck makers.

"That strategy worked to some extent, but the complexities of integrating all those brands, supply chains and different designs make VW very complicated to operate," Daniel Harrison, senior automotive analyst at the London-based Ultima Media, told DW.
Can Volkswagen's 'legacy' help restore its former glory?
Why the VW model broke
Although Volkswagen survived the 2015 Dieselgate emissions scandal without suffering lasting financial damage, the company incurred massive costs and soon faced a new set of problems.

The company was slow to transition its production to electric vehicles (EVs) — just as Chinese EV makers gained serious traction and a technological edge. That delay contributed to slower sales in China, which accounted for a third of total VW sales, as well as softening demand in Europe and other key markets.

VW also repeated a mistake made by the US auto industry decades earlier. In the 1960s and 1970s, the Big Three — Ford, GM, and Chrysler (now part of Stellantis) — were bloated and slow to adapt when Japanese and European competitors began eating into their market share.
By the time US carmakers shifted toward leaner production methods, a decade had passed, and they had fallen significantly behind, noted Ostertag.
Toyota, which produces a similar number of vehicles as VW, operates with nearly half the workers by relying more on suppliers, higher automation, and a simpler management structure.

blocks.caption: Four German plants, including this one at Zwickau, are facing closureImage: AAPimages/Wehnert/picture alliance

blocks.text: In a research note, auto industry analyst Matthias Schmidt pointed to another factor: the "stranglehold" that trade unions and a key shareholder have over VW. This, he said, had helped cause "years of neglect in readjusting workforce numbers."

The northern German state of Lower Saxony — home to Volkswagen's global headquarters in Wolfsburg — holds 20% of voting rights in the company, can veto major decisions, and has previously pressured executives not to close plants or lay off staff, notably during the Dieselgate and COVID supply chain crises. It's ramping up the pressure this time, too.
Over the decades, Germany's powerful unions, meanwhile, have repeatedly held out for high wage increases and generous benefits, which have made VW staff among the best-paid autoworkers in the world.

blocks.caption: With plants in Thailand and Brazil, China's BYD opening a factory in HungaryImage: Jin Haoyuan/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: Is VW's turnaround plan enough?
Analysts warn that the company may have to cut more than the annual €4 billion the firm hopes to save to secure its future.

The current proposals to cut 50,000 additional jobs, they say, will bring savings and help improve short-term profitability. But VW's underlying cost base and slow decision-making culture mean deeper, more radical reforms may well be needed.

VW should "invest more heavily in automation," Ostertag told DW, adding that it would allow the carmaker to "better compete with leaner firms," such as China's BYD, one of the fastest-growing EV brands in Europe.

Analysts say VW has lagged peers in plant automation levels but has stepped up investments in robotics and digital upgrades for its EV production. The company is also planning its first sub-€20,000 EV next year.

With China responsible for around 30% of VW's global vehicle output, Harrison predicts more production shifts to Asia and the potential to share VW's European plants with Chinese EV producers, a move previously seen as "unthinkable."
Chinese EV maker BYD goes Europe
German government, EU offer a lifeline
On the policy front, the German government is providing subsidies and loans for domestic EV battery plants to help cut reliance on Chinese imports.

The European Union, meanwhile, is advancing the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). The IAA is meant to boost the bloc's competitiveness and shield strategic industries from unfair competition from China.
The EU has already imposed tariffs of up to 45% on Chinese-made EVs. But they are far below the 100% levies that the US charges, which have largely shut Chinese competitors out of the US auto market.
Historian Niall Ferguson from Harvard University warned that Europe has been slow to respond to China's strategy of giving huge subsidies to EV makers that help undercut European rivals.
"Unless there's radical change, I predict: Europeans will be driving Chinese cars on a massive scale very soon," Ferguson told Germany's Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper earlier this year.

During the same interview, economist Moritz Schularick, President of the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, suggested using market access as leverage — only allowing Chinese brands to sell in Europe if they produce locally.
Schularick responded provocatively when questioned on VW's long-term future, predicting that Germany's auto giant would "likely be bought by a Chinese car maker like BYD."
Editor's note: The article, originally published on July 7, 2026, has been updated to include the VW Supervisory Board's backing for a restructuring plan calling for an additional 50,000 job cuts.
